0.title: Aider vs. Cline: Technical Comparison & Architectural Evaluation
0.content: This document provides a technical blueprint and comparative analysis of Aider and Cline, two top-tier, open-source (Apache-2.0) AI coding assistants operating on a “Bring Your Own Key” (BYOK) model. While both tools leverage frontier LLMs for code generation, they cater to distinct developer workflows, execution primitives, and repository topologies.

1.title: 1. Executive Summary & Core Paradigm Comparison
1.content: Establishing an automated, AI-assisted development workflow requires balancing execution velocity, codebase context retention, and system safety boundaries. | Aider: A terminal-native pair programmer optimized for Git automation, strict token economy, and continuous inline code generation. | Cline: An autonomous, agentic workspace operating inside IDE extensions (and CLI/desktop apps) capable of multi-step planning, parallel subagent spawning, and automated visual browser debugging. | . +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Developer Task | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------+ | +-----------------------+-----------------------+ | v v +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Aider Loop | Cline Loop | - Terminal CLI | - IDE Sidebar / App | - Strict Repo Map | - Plan & Act Mode | - Auto Git Commit | - Visual Approval | - Fast Sequential | - Browser / MCP Ops | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ . Technical Feature Matrix . | Feature Dimension | Aider | Cline | . | Primary Interface | Terminal / CLI (native command line) | VS Code / JetBrains extension, CLI 2.0, Desktop App | . | Execution Architecture | Sequential Pair Programmer | Multi-step Autonomous Agent (Parallel Subagents) | . | Safety & State Control | Git-Native (automatic diffs & local commits) | Visual Step-by-Step Approval (File & Shell prompts) | . | Codebase Context | Structural Repository Map (tree-sitter AST) | Dynamic Mentioning (@file, @folder) & Dynamic Indexing | . | Token Efficiency | High (optimized AST maps minimize prompt bloat) | Moderate (continuous deep file reads consume higher context) | . | Specialized Capabilities | Voice-to-code, Architect/Editor dual-model pipeline | MCP (Model Context Protocol) support, Browser Automation | . | License & Ownership | Apache-2.0 (Maintained by Paul Gauthier) | Apache-2.0 (Maintained by Cline Bot Inc.) | .

2.title: 2. Architectural Deep-Dive & Key Differentiators
2.content: A. Context Mapping & Token Efficiency . Aider: AST-Based Repository Mapping . Aider uses tree-sitter to parse the codebase into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), extracting function signatures, class definitions, and variable references. It generates a compressed Repo Map that fits within a small fraction of the context window. \[\text{Context Overhead}_{\text{Aider}} = \mathcal{O}(\text{AST Signatures}) \ll \mathcal{O}(\text{Full File Contents})\] This enables Aider to reason over large repositories ($>10,000 \text{ LOC}$) without exhausting LLM context limits or spiking API costs. Cline: Dynamic Mentions & Act-Phase Context Inflation . Cline reads full file contents into memory when referenced via prompts or when navigating directories during its “Act” loop. While this provides detailed visibility into specific submodules, it scales context consumption linearly with file size, making token discipline essential for long-running sessions. B. Workflow Guardrails: Git Auto-Commits vs. Visual Approvals . Aider Workflow: [User Prompt] ---> [LLM Diff Generation] ---> [Apply File Edits] ---> [Auto Git Commit] Cline Workflow: [User Prompt] ---> [Plan Generation] ---> [User Approval] ---> [Action Proposed] | v [Visual Diff Approval] | v [Execute File Modification] . | Aider’s Git-Native Strategy: Assumes all work takes place within a Git repository. Once an edit is generated, Aider creates a local Git commit with conventional commit syntax. If an output is incorrect, the developer rolls back using git undo or standard Git branching. | Cline’s Visual Step-Approval: Operates as a state machine. Every proposed terminal command or file write pauses execution and presents a colored diff in the UI, requiring explicit user approval before changing workspace state. | . C. Advanced Capabilities: Multi-Model Pipelines & Extensibility . Aider Architect Mode . Aider supports a two-model pipeline that decouples high-level reasoning from code syntax generation: . | Architect Model (e.g., Claude 3.7 Sonnet / Claude 3.5 Opus): Evaluates the codebase map, plans logic changes, and drafts solution pseudo-code. | Editor Model (e.g., Claude 3.5 Haiku / DeepSeek-V3): Receives the architect’s output and generates the raw source code diff. | . \text{Cost}_{\text{Pipeline}} = C_{\text{Architect}}(\text{Planning Tokens}) + C_{\text{Editor}}(\text{Syntax Tokens}) . This dual-model approach lowers API costs while preserving reasoning quality on complex refactoring tasks. Cline Agentic Suite (MCP, Browser Automation, Subagents) . | Model Context Protocol (MCP): Native support for MCP servers allows Cline to query external PostgreSQL databases, interact with Slack, or pull live telemetry directly into its execution loop. | Browser Automation: Launches headless/headed browser instances to inspect local dev servers (e.g., http://localhost:3000), take DOM screenshots, and debug UI components visually. | Subagents (v3.58+): Spawns isolated background subagents to solve parallel tasks (e.g., running unit tests in one process while updating API types in another). | .

3.title: 3. Decision Framework: Choosing the Right Assistant
3.content: +-----------------------+ | Which Tool To Use? | +-----------------------+ | +-----------------------+-----------------------+ | v v [ Terminal / CLI User? ] [ Graphical IDE User? ] [ Massive Legacy Repo? ] [ Visual App / Web UI? ] [ Low Token Budget? ] [ Needs MCP Tooling? ] | v v +----------------+ +----------------+ | Use AIDER | Use CLINE | +----------------+ +----------------+ . Choose Aider if: . | You work primarily in CLI environments (Neovim, Tmux, Alacritty, or remote SSH nodes). | You manage large codebases where AST-based repository mapping prevents context window exhaustion. | You prefer an automated Git commit history for rapid iteration and rollback. | . Choose Cline if: . | You develop in VS Code or JetBrains and prefer a visual diff panel before changing files. | You require automated frontend visual testing via integrated browser controls. | You want to connect your coding assistant to enterprise infrastructure using Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations. | .

4.title: 4. Key Takeaways
4.content: . | Model Neutrality: Both tools utilize a BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) model and support leading frontier models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1/V3, Ollama). | Context Efficiency: Aider excels at low-token repository navigation via AST mapping, whereas Cline provides deeper single-file reasoning at higher context cost. | Execution Safety: Aider enforces state safety through automated local Git commits, while Cline relies on interactive user approvals per action. ``` | .

6.title: Claude Code Masterclass Guide
6.content: Reference lecture by Michele Torti: YouTube . This masterclass explains how to progress from beginner-level Claude Code usage to building agentic workflows and automated AI systems.

7.title: Course Overview and Roadmap
7.content: The masterclass is organized into five core modules: . | Foundations — Installation, workspace hosting, permissions, built-in commands, and project context through CLAUDE.md. | Customization — Custom skills, slash commands, lifecycle hooks, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations. | Prompt Engineering — Structuring inputs for reliable and consistent Claude Code outputs. | Agentic Workflows — Sub-agents, agent teams, workflow optimization, and continuous deployment. | Real-World Builds — End-to-end implementation of practical projects. | .

10.content: Claude Code can be used across several integrated development environments and execution environments. | Environment | Main strength | Main limitation | . | Visual Studio Code | General-purpose IDE with file navigation and official Anthropic extension | Requires IDE installation and workspace setup | . | Cursor | AI-focused coding environment with native AI features | Users may pay separately for Cursor and Claude usage | . | Google Antigravity | VS Code-like environment with access to Google’s ecosystem | Adds another product and configuration layer | . | Terminal CLI | Lightweight, direct command-line access | Less approachable for beginners | . | Claude Desktop | Familiar desktop interface | Less visual control over project files and directories | . Visual Studio Code . Visual Studio Code is presented as the recommended standard IDE for beginners. It provides: . | A file and folder explorer. | A project workspace. | An integrated terminal. | An extension system. | Visual access to Claude Code. | A place to inspect and review generated files. | . Installing Claude Code in an IDE . The general installation workflow is: . | Download and open Visual Studio Code or Google Antigravity. | Open the Extensions panel. | Search for Claude Code. | Verify that the publisher is Anthropic. | Install the official extension. | Authenticate using a Claude subscription or API credentials. | Open the target project folder. | Start Claude Code within that workspace. | . Keyboard shortcuts for opening the Extensions panel are: . | Operating system | Shortcut | . | Windows/Linux | Ctrl+Shift+X | . | macOS | Cmd+Shift+X | . Workspace Scope . Claude Code operates within the currently opened project folder. The active workspace defines the files and directories Claude Code can inspect and modify. +----------------------+ | Open Project Folder | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Start Claude Code | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Inspect Project | Files and Folders | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Build, Edit, Test, | and Review | +----------------------+ .

11.title: Interface Controls and Permission Modes
11.content: Claude Code provides multiple permission modes that control how aggressively it can edit files or execute terminal commands. | Permission mode | Behavior | Recommended use | . | Ask before edits | Requests approval before writing or editing files | Review-oriented workflows | . | Edit automatically | Applies edits without asking for every individual change | Routine, low-risk tasks | . | Plan mode | Creates a structured implementation plan before execution | Complex or high-impact tasks | . | Bypass permissions | Skips confirmation prompts for edits and command execution | Controlled sandboxes only | . Ask Before Edits . Claude Code requests approval before making file changes or executing certain actions. This mode is useful when: . | Reviewing unfamiliar code. | Working with sensitive repositories. | Learning how Claude Code operates. | Making high-impact changes. | Maintaining strict human oversight. | . Edit Automatically . Claude Code applies file edits without asking for approval before every change. This mode is useful for: . | Small changes. | Repetitive edits. | Well-understood tasks. | Low-risk project maintenance. | . The user should still inspect the final result. Plan Mode . Plan mode separates planning from execution. User Request | v +----------------------+ | Claude Creates Plan | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | User Reviews Plan | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | User Approves Plan | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Claude Executes | Approved Work | +----------------------+ . Plan mode is useful when: . | The task affects several files. | The implementation requires design decisions. | The change is difficult to reverse. | The user wants to review the approach first. | The project contains strict conventions or business rules. | . Bypass Permissions . Bypass permissions skips confirmation prompts for edits and terminal commands. This setting may be convenient, but it increases the potential impact of mistakes. Claude Code may be able to: . | Modify files. | Delete or overwrite content. | Execute shell commands. | Install dependencies. | Access connected tools. | Change project state without asking. | . Use this mode only in controlled environments where the consequences of unwanted changes are understood and limited. More Convenience | v Fewer Approval Prompts | v Greater Potential Impact | v Requires Stronger Oversight . Effort Control . Claude Code includes an effort setting with three levels: . | Effort level | Expected behavior | Trade-off | . | Low | Faster and lighter processing | May provide less analysis | . | Medium | Balanced reasoning and speed | Recommended general-purpose setting | . | High | More extensive reasoning and verification | May consume more usage and take longer | .

12.title: Essential Built-In Slash Commands
12.content: Slash commands provide direct access to common Claude Code operations. | Command | Purpose | Description | . | /clear | Reset conversation | Clears the current conversation context | . | /context | Inspect token usage | Displays context usage and its breakdown | . | /compact | Compress conversation | Summarizes earlier messages to free context space | . | /init | Initialize project instructions | Inspects an existing repository and generates CLAUDE.md | . | /prime | Refresh project context | Loads project instructions, skills, and commands | . | /hooks | Manage hooks | Opens the hook configuration interface | . /clear . The /clear command starts a fresh conversation context. It is useful when: . | The current conversation contains irrelevant information. | The user is starting an unrelated task. | The conversation has become confusing. | The user wants to reduce accumulated context. | . Clearing the conversation does not delete project files. /context . The /context command displays how the available context is being used. A context report may include: . | System instructions. | Tool definitions. | Skills. | Conversation messages. | MCP tools. | Reserved buffer. | Remaining free space. | . /compact . The /compact command summarizes an existing conversation so that work can continue with less context consumption. Long Conversation | v +----------------------+ | Preserve Important | Decisions and Tasks | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Generate Compact | Conversation Summary | +----------------------+ | v Continue Work with Additional Context Space . Important project requirements should be stored in files such as CLAUDE.md or directive documents rather than only in a conversation. /init . The /init command analyzes an existing project and generates an initial CLAUDE.md file. It is most useful when: . | A repository already contains code. | The project lacks persistent Claude Code instructions. | The user wants Claude Code to document the existing structure. | The user wants an initial project context file to review and refine. | . /prime . The /prime command refreshes the session with project-specific context. Depending on the configuration, this may include: . | CLAUDE.md. | Custom skills. | Custom slash commands. | Project conventions. | Relevant documentation. | . /hooks . The /hooks command opens the hook configuration interface and allows the user to inspect or modify event-driven actions.

13.title: Project Memory: The CLAUDE.md File
13.content: The CLAUDE.md file acts as the project instruction manual for Claude Code. It provides persistent context about: . | What the project does. | Which technologies it uses. | How files should be organized. | Which rules Claude must follow. | Which actions require approval. | What outputs are expected. | . New Claude Code Session | v Read CLAUDE.md | v Understand Project Context | v Apply Rules and Guardrails | v Execute User Task . The Four Pillars of CLAUDE.md . A useful CLAUDE.md file should cover four major areas. | Pillar | Purpose | Typical content | . | Product description | Explains what the project does | Business purpose, users, objectives | . | Technology stack | Describes the implementation environment | Languages, frameworks, APIs, services | . | Rules and guardrails | Defines required and prohibited behavior | Naming, formatting, security, design rules | . | Folder structure | Explains where files belong | Directories, output locations, file conventions | . Product Description . The product description explains: . | What the application or business does. | Who uses it. | What problem it solves. | What the main project objectives are. | Which outputs the project should produce. | . Technology Stack . The technology-stack section records the tools used by the project, such as: . | Programming languages. | Frameworks. | Databases. | APIs. | Hosting services. | Automation platforms. | Package managers. | Build tools. | . Rules and Guardrails . Rules and guardrails help Claude Code produce more consistent results. They may define: . | Naming conventions. | Formatting standards. | Color palettes. | Font choices. | Required libraries. | Prohibited dependencies. | Security requirements. | File-placement rules. | Testing expectations. | Content tone. | Business logic constraints. | . Folder Structure . The folder-structure section explains where different types of files should be placed. A well-defined structure prevents files from being scattered across the workspace.

14.title: Project Organization
14.content: Three-Layer Architecture . For a new project, the masterclass recommends separating instructions, decisions, and execution. my-project/ ├── CLAUDE.md ├── .env ├── directives/ ├── decisions/ ├── execution/ └── tmp/ . | Directory or file | Purpose | . | CLAUDE.md | Persistent project instructions | . | .env | API keys and sensitive configuration | . | directives/ | SOPs, instructions, and objectives | . | decisions/ | Architectural decisions and decision trees | . | execution/ | Executable code, scripts, and build artifacts | . | tmp/ | Temporary generation outputs | . Directives . Directives explain what should be done. They may contain: . | Objectives. | Inputs. | Expected outputs. | Step-by-step procedures. | Edge cases. | Business rules. | Quality requirements. | . Decisions . Decision documents explain how choices should be made. They may contain: . | Conditional logic. | Selection criteria. | Architectural decisions. | Policies. | Routing rules. | Escalation conditions. | . Execution . Execution contains the operational implementation. It may contain: . | Scripts. | Automation workflows. | Build files. | Data-processing code. | Integration logic. | Generated operational artifacts. | . Environment Variables . The .env file stores sensitive configuration such as: . | API keys. | Passwords. | Authentication tokens. | Service credentials. | Environment-specific settings. | . Do not commit secrets to a public repository. CLAUDE.md -> Project Instructions directives/ -> Business Procedures decisions/ -> Logic and Policies execution/ -> Operational Implementation .env -> Secrets and Configuration .

15.title: Initializing a New Project
15.content: Method 1: Create CLAUDE.md First . For a new project: . | Create a project folder. | Create a CLAUDE.md file. | Describe the project. | Define the technology stack. | Add rules and guardrails. | Describe the folder structure. | Ask Claude Code to initialize the project. | Review the generated directories and files. | . Create Empty Workspace | v Write CLAUDE.md | v Define Architecture and Rules | v Ask Claude Code to Initialize | v Create Directories and Files | v Review Workspace . A generalized initialization prompt is: . Initialize this project based on the instructions in CLAUDE.md. Create the required folder structure, configuration files, and initial documentation. Do not introduce technologies that are not specified in CLAUDE.md. Explain what you create and identify anything that requires my approval. Method 2: Initialize an Existing Repository . For an existing repository, run: . /init . Claude Code analyzes the repository and generates an initial CLAUDE.md file. The workflow is: . | Open the existing project folder. | Start Claude Code. | Run /init. | Allow Claude Code to inspect the repository. | Review the generated CLAUDE.md. | Correct inaccurate assumptions. | Add missing rules and conventions. | Continue working with the refined project instructions. | . Existing Project | v Run /init | v Inspect Files and Folders | v Generate CLAUDE.md | v Review and Refine | v Continue Project Work . | Project scenario | Recommended method | . | New project with no structure | Create CLAUDE.md, then initialize the project | . | Existing project with files and folders | Run /init, then review the generated file | .

17.title: Skills Architecture
17.content: Skills are reusable, step-by-step instruction packages that guide Claude Code through complex procedures. Examples include: . | Frontend design. | Diagram creation. | Lead extraction. | Data analysis. | Content generation. | Research workflows. | Deployment procedures. | Testing and verification. | . A skill allows a procedure to be reused without rewriting the complete prompt every time. Skill Directory Layout . Custom skills are stored in the .claude/skills/ directory.claude/ └── skills/ └── lead-generation-system/ ├── SKILL.md ├── references/ └── scripts/ . | Path | Purpose | . | SKILL.md | Main skill instructions and metadata | . | references/ | Templates, examples, guidelines, and supporting documents | . | scripts/ | Optional Python, JavaScript, or shell automation scripts | . Use a descriptive directory name instead of a generic / directory. Anatomy of a SKILL.md File . A skill file typically contains YAML metadata followed by Markdown instructions. *** name: lead-generation-system description: Extracts and qualifies business leads from a target market. *** # Lead Generation System ## Prerequisites - Apify API token configured in `.env`. - Required scraping permissions. - Target niche and location. - Desired result limit. ## Inputs - Target niche. - Geographic area. - Maximum number of leads. - Qualification criteria. ## Procedure 1. Fetch target leads using the configured scraper. 2. Filter results to retain entries containing website and phone details. 3. Extract content from home, about, and service pages. 4. Analyze the extracted value propositions. 5. Export the cleaned dataset to CSV. ## Outputs - Qualified lead dataset. - Source URLs. - Contact information. - Qualification notes. - CSV export. ## Quality Checks - Confirm that required fields are present. - Remove duplicate businesses. - Verify that URLs are valid. - Record failed extraction attempts. Skill Design Principles . A reliable skill should specify: . | Its purpose. | When it should be triggered. | Required inputs. | Prerequisites. | Step-by-step procedure. | Expected outputs. | Error-handling behavior. | Quality checks. | File locations. | Security requirements. | .

18.title: Automated Skill Creation and Evaluation
18.content: Skill Creation . The skill-creator workflow can be used to generate a new skill from an existing successful procedure. A skill may be created by: . | Installing an official skill-creation plugin. | Asking Claude Code to convert a successful workflow into a reusable skill. | Extracting repeated instructions from a project. | Turning a manual SOP into structured instructions. | . Evaluation Framework . Automated evaluations help determine whether a skill: . | Recognizes the correct user intent. | Follows the required procedure. | Produces the expected output. | Respects formatting requirements. | Handles edge cases. | Avoids triggering for unrelated requests. | . A possible evaluation structure is: .claude/ └── skills/ └── lead-generation-system/ ├── SKILL.md └── evals/ ├── eval.json └── trigger_eval.json . | Evaluation file | Purpose | . | eval.json | Tests the skill’s output and execution behavior | . | trigger_eval.json | Tests whether the skill triggers for appropriate prompts | . A typical evaluation loop is: . Create Skill | v Run Evaluation Cases | v Measure Pass/Fail Results | v Identify Weaknesses | v Update SKILL.md | v Run Evaluations Again . Evaluation metrics may include: . | Pass rate. | Output completeness. | Format compliance. | Intent-recognition accuracy. | Error-handling quality. | Correct file placement. | Required-field coverage. | .

19.title: Custom Slash Commands
19.content: Custom slash commands provide short commands for invoking predefined skills or workflows. Command Directory Layout . Custom commands are stored in .claude/commands/.claude/ └── commands/ ├── generate-titles.md └── lead-gen.md . Command Mapping Example . The file .claude/commands/lead-gen.md may contain: . When the user calls `/lead-gen`, invoke the `lead-generation-system` skill. Ask for: - Target niche. - Geographic location. - Desired result limit. Then execute the skill and save the output to the project's designated output directory. Invoking a Custom Command . Once the command is configured, the user can run: . /lead-gen . The command can then: . | Ask for missing inputs. | Load the relevant skill. | Execute the defined workflow. | Validate the output. | Save the results to the correct location. | . /lead-gen | v Load Lead Generation Skill | v Collect Required Inputs | v Run Workflow | v Validate Results | v Save Output .

20.title: Event-Driven Hooks
20.content: Hooks execute automatic actions at specific Claude Code lifecycle events. They can be used to: . | Validate commands before execution. | Format files after edits. | Run tests after code changes. | Send notifications when a task finishes. | Record errors. | Trigger cleanup procedures. | Enforce project rules. | . Hook Configuration . Hooks may be configured in a Claude Code settings file such as .claude/settings.json. A conceptual notification example is: . { "hooks": { "post_response": [ { "type": "command", "command": "osascript -e 'display notification \"Claude Code task complete!\" with title \"Claude Code\"'" } ] } } . Platform note: The osascript command is specific to macOS. Windows and Linux require different notification mechanisms. Common Lifecycle Triggers . | Trigger | Typical use | . | Pre-tool use | Validate or authorize an action before execution | . | Post-tool use | Format files, update logs, or perform cleanup | . | Post-tool-use failure | Send alerts or record diagnostic information | . | Post-response | Notify the user when Claude finishes a task | . Hook Flow . Claude Code Event | v +----------------------+ | Match Hook Trigger | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Execute Command or | Automation Script | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Continue, Notify, | Log, or Block Action | +----------------------+ . Hook Safety . Hooks can execute commands automatically, so they should be designed carefully. Recommended safeguards include: . | Validate input before executing commands. | Avoid destructive shell commands. | Restrict access to sensitive files. | Log important actions. | Handle failures explicitly. | Test hooks in a sandbox. | Require approval for high-impact operations. | Avoid embedding credentials directly in configuration files. | .

21.title: Formatting and Maintenance Notes
21.content: . | Use CLAUDE.md consistently for project-level instructions. | Use uppercase SKILL.md for skill files unless the project convention specifies otherwise. | Use descriptive directory names. | Keep tables compact enough to render on mobile screens. | Use blank lines before and after every table. | Do not place blank lines inside a table unless the table is intentionally split. | Keep each table cell concise. | Use <br> only when a cell genuinely requires multiple lines. | Prefer separate tables over very wide tables. | Keep code fences closed and separated from surrounding paragraphs. | Use backticks for commands, filenames, paths, and code identifiers. | Avoid using HTML line breaks inside ordinary prose. | .

23.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
23.title: Decision Models: Jev, AnyJev, and the Decision Layer for AI Systems
23.content: Reference: Introducing Decision 1.0: Open Decision Foundation Models . Decision models are a new class of language models optimized to make fast, typed, probability-bearing decisions rather than generate free-form text. They sit between an application’s understanding of a request and its next action: given a state, a question, and candidate options, they return calibrated distributions over those options. The central pattern is: . \[\text{State} + \text{Questions} + \text{Criteria} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distributions}\] This document covers the Jev-style decision-model interface, the architecture and trade-offs of open decision models, the AnyJev training-free and self-distilled approaches, calibration, deployment, and practical use in agents, search, routing, and evaluation.

24.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
24.title: Part 1: Foundations
24.content: What is a decision model? . A decision model is a model that consumes a context or state and returns a structured decision over a predefined set of alternatives. Instead of producing a paragraph of reasoning or a natural-language answer, it scores candidates and returns probabilities. A typical decision request contains: . | State: the evidence or context to evaluate, such as a support ticket, document, agent trace, search result, or user request. | Question: what the system needs to determine. | Candidates or criteria: the allowed answers, actions, labels, or rubric levels. | Output: a selected option plus a probability distribution over all options. | . For example, given a customer message about a duplicate charge, a decision model may answer: . | Which team should handle this: billing, technical, or sales? | Did the customer request a refund? | How urgent is the issue: can wait, this week, or today? | . The model returns a distribution such as billing: 0.91, technical: 0.07, sales: 0.02, allowing the application to route the request, set an escalation threshold, or prioritize a queue. vllm-sr . Why not just use an LLM? . A generative LLM can perform classification by prompting it to output a label. However, for high-volume operational decisions, this approach has several drawbacks: . | Concern | Generative LLM classification | Decision model | . | Output format | Text that may need parsing or validation | Typed decision with option probabilities | . | Latency | Often requires autoregressive generation | Can score candidates in one forward pass | . | Cost | Higher when generating reasoning tokens | Lower when decisions are read from logits or a single prefill | . | Confidence | Often poorly calibrated without extra work | Designed to expose probabilities for policy decisions | . | Flexibility | Broad reasoning and generation capability | Focused on choosing among supplied alternatives | . | Best fit | Open-ended reasoning, planning, writing | Routing, gating, triage, scoring, policy checks | . Decision models do not replace LLMs. They separate the frequent, short-horizon decisions that an application must make from the slower System-2 work of planning, reasoning, query generation, and answer composition. arxiv . System 1 versus System 2 . The terminology comes from a dual-process view of cognition: . | System 1 is fast, automatic, and low-effort. In AI systems, this maps to immediate decisions such as “route this ticket,” “is this relevant?”, or “should this action be allowed?” | System 2 is slower, deliberate, and effortful. In AI systems, this maps to multi-step planning, tool use, complex reasoning, and generating a final answer. | . SearchJev explicitly applies this split to search agents: a small decision model handles repeated short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions, while a larger System-2 model handles planning, query generation, and answer composition. arxiv . User request | v +---------------------+ | System 1: Decision | Fast, typed, probabilistic | - relevance? | - enough evidence? | - next action? | +---------------------+ | confident |--------------------------+ | uncertain | v v +---------------------+ +---------------------+ | Execute fast action | System 2: Reasoner | or continue loop | - plan | +---------------------+ | - generate queries | - compose answer | +---------------------+ . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the dual-system architecture described by SearchJev. arxiv .

25.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
25.title: Part 2: The Jev Decision Interface
25.content: Three decision types . The Jev-style interface defines three primary decision types. Decision 1.0 uses the names Choice, Noul, and Score. vllm-sr . | Type | Question form | Output | Typical use | . | Choice | “Which option is best?” | One selected candidate and a distribution over candidates | Routing, action selection, classification | . | Noul | “Is this condition true?” | Probability of yes | Policy gates, evidence checks, escalation | . | Score | “Rate this on an ordered rubric.” | Distribution over ordered levels and an expected score | Urgency, quality, severity, review rubrics | . A Choice is appropriate when exactly one option should be selected. A Noul is appropriate for a yes/no condition; multiple Noul questions can implement multi-label checks, though their probabilities need not sum to one. A Score is appropriate when the levels have a meaningful order, such as can wait < this week < today. vllm-sr . Example: customer support . Consider a customer who reports a damaged parcel and asks for a replacement today. Decision 1.0 illustrates three questions over the same state: vllm-sr . | Type | Ask the model | Use the answer | . | Choice | Which team should handle this: delivery, billing, or technical support? | Route using the selected candidate ID and its distribution | . | Noul | Does the customer request action today? | Use the yes probability to decide whether to escalate | . | Score | Rate urgency: can wait, this week, today | Prioritize the queue using the level distribution and expected score | . The important design point is that the application—not the model—owns the action policy. The model supplies probabilities; the application decides what probability threshold triggers escalation, refund approval, human review, or another workflow branch. vllm-sr . Candidate descriptions instead of fixed labels . A decision model does not need a fixed vocabulary of task labels. Candidates can be short identifiers such as billing or technical, or richer descriptions such as “Payments and refunds” and “Product faults.” . Decision 1.0’s Lux model uses a shared candidate readout: all candidates for one question are scored in a single forward pass, and candidate descriptions come from the request rather than a fixed label set. This makes the same model usable for routing, tool selection, policy checks, and evaluation without retraining the head for every new task. vllm-sr . Batch decisions . Real workflows rarely need one decision at a time. A support record may require a destination, refund check, escalation decision, and priority score. Applying those four questions to 128 records produces 512 decisions. Decision 1.0’s Kai and Lex native Python API accepts up to 128 independent requests and 512 total decisions per local SDK batch submission, preserving request and question order. The runtime groups work into physical batches; the 512 figure describes submission capacity, not simultaneous forward passes or measured throughput. vllm-sr .

26.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
26.title: Part 3: Model Architectures
26.content: Decision 1.0 family . Decision 1.0 is a family of six open-weight Decision Foundation Models released by the vLLM Semantic Router team. The family uses two architectural branches. vllm-sr . | Model | Built for | Input budget | . | Decision-1.0-Kai-0.6B | Compact general-purpose routing, conditions, and action selection | 1,024 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Lex-0.6B | Operational decisions: customer service, invoices, security incidents, agent traces | 1,024 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Eos-0.8B | Smallest hybrid decoder tier for longer evidence | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Sol-2B | Greater capacity for decisions over extended context | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Nox-4B | Combining conditions, applying rules, and choosing actions | 16,384 tokens | . | Decision-1.0-Lux-9B | Largest model and strongest overall result on the released decision suite | 16,384 tokens | . The input budget covers the complete state, question, and candidate descriptions. vllm-sr . Encoder branch: Kai and Lex . Kai and Lex use three bidirectional encoder paths built on Vela. Each path has separate interaction layers and readouts for Choice, Noul, and Score. vllm-sr . Conceptually: . State + question + candidates | +------------------+------------------+ | | Choice path Noul path Score path | | candidate logits yes probability ordered level logits | | distribution probability level distribution . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the three-path encoder design. Bidirectional encoders are naturally suited to classification because every token can attend to every other token in the input, which is useful when the answer depends on relationships across the whole state. vllm-sr . Decoder branch: Eos, Sol, Nox, and Lux . Eos, Sol, Nox, and Lux adapt Qwen3.5 text backbones. They combine Gated DeltaNet with full attention and use a shared candidate head. vllm-sr . This hybrid design reflects a common trade-off: . | Full attention provides strong context modeling and is effective for long-range dependencies. | Gated DeltaNet is a more efficient sequence-mixing mechanism that can reduce the cost of processing long contexts. | A shared candidate head scores each supplied candidate, allowing the candidate set to vary per request. | . Lux-9B scores all candidates for one question in a single forward pass; independent questions are processed in batches. vllm-sr . Published benchmark results . Decision 1.0 reports results across 3,766 scored decisions in a selected 54-task suite covering decisions, composition, reading, inference, and transfer. vllm-sr . | Model | Overall score | . | Lux-9B | 76.94 | . | Nox-4B | 73.09 | . | Sol-2B | 66.32 | . | Eos-0.8B | 61.89 | . | Kai-0.6B | 53.52 | . | Kev-9B, displayed open-model reference | 71.89 | . | Hosted Jev reference | 81.05 | . Lux leads the displayed open-model references on this suite, while the hosted Jev reference remains higher overall. Lux reaches 84.10 on Decisions and 91.46 on Inference; Nox leads the displayed Decision models on Composition. These are results from the release’s selected tasks and weighted overall metric, so they should not be treated as universal rankings. vllm-sr .

27.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
27.title: Part 4: AnyJev
27.content: What AnyJev does . AnyJev is an open-source framework that turns an LLM into a Jev-style decision model. It provides typed decisions and probability distributions without requiring generated text to be parsed. github . AnyJev provides two main paths: . | Training-free Decider: works with any open causal language model, with no training and no labels. | Self-distilled Tacit: uses checkpoints trained through self-distillation so the model can answer in one forward pass. github | . The problem with raw label logits . A naive way to build a decision model from an LLM is to prompt it with candidate labels and read the next-token logits for each label. This is simple but problematic: . | The result can change when the order of options changes. | The model may have a prior preference for certain label strings. | The resulting probabilities may be poorly calibrated. | . AnyJev’s L0 readout addresses both issues without labels by averaging position bias over rotations of the options and dividing out the label prior. github . L0 rotation readout . At level L0, AnyJev reads a K-option choice once per rotation of the options. Each rotation changes the ordering of candidates, and the readout aggregates the resulting distributions to reduce order sensitivity. For each rotation r of the K candidate options: Read logits for each option label Convert logits to an option distribution Aggregate distributions across rotations Remove label prior Return final calibrated decision distribution . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the rotation-based readout. The repository reports that, on Qwen3-8B for a 20-way BANKING77 task with 300 test items, L0 reduced answer flips when options were reversed from 0.230 to 0.073, improved accuracy from 0.747 to 0.803, and reduced expected calibration error from 0.240 to 0.184. github . The most consequential improvement is automation capacity: the share of decisions confident enough to automate at no more than 5% error rose from 7.7% with raw logits to 46.3% with L0, using no labels. github . Rotation budget . Running all K rotations is expensive for large candidate sets. AnyJev’s rotation budget reads only as many rotations as the decision needs. The stopping threshold is calibrated against AnyJev’s own full-cycle answer, so it does not require labels. The repository reports that, at a certified 1% disagreement, it read 7.2 rotations instead of 18, yielding 2.2 times more decisions per second on vLLM and 2.3 to 2.7 times more on transformers, with accuracy unchanged. github . Tacit self-distilled models . Tacit models are trained by self-distillation: the model learns to produce, in one forward pass, the answers it would reach when it reasons. No human labels and no separate teacher model are involved. github . The trade-off is: . | One-forward mode: fast and cheap; one prefill per decision. | Adaptive mode: low-confidence decisions are escalated to the model’s own reasoning, then read as a label distribution after the reasoning step. | . Adaptive escalation is bounded by configuration: . | Argument | Default | Meaning | . | adaptive | False | Send low-confidence decisions to the model’s own reasoning | . | tau | 0.5 | Low confidence when the log-probability gap between the top two options is below this value | . | max_cot_share | 0.2 | Maximum share of the recent decision window allowed to escalate | . | cot_window | 1000 | Number of recent decisions counted by the escalation cap | . | cot_max_tokens | 8192 | Reasoning budget for one escalated decision | . | engine | "transformers" | Also supports in-process vLLM or a remote vllm serve endpoint | . The cap matters operationally: even if traffic becomes difficult, at most max_cot_share of the last cot_window decisions escalate. Every escalation is reported through route == "cot", and the first-pass result is retained. github . Tacit results . AnyJev reports Tacit accuracy on the public JevBench set, which has 231 items, and the bev-decision test split, which has 46,320 items. github . | Model | Base model | JevBench public | Adaptive | bev-decision test | Adaptive | . | Tacit-9B | Qwen3.5-9B | 0.823 | 0.887, 15.2% escalated | 0.727 | 0.755, 18.1% escalated | . | Tacit-8B | Qwen3-8B | 0.736 | — | 0.663 | — | . | Tacit-4B | Qwen3-4B | 0.723 | 0.758, 14.3% escalated | 0.663 | 0.704, 17.8% escalated | . | Tacit-2B | Qwen3.5-2B | 0.671 | — | 0.626 | — | . | Tacit-1.7B | Qwen3-1.7B | 0.619 | — | 0.598 | — | . For Tacit-9B, escalation added an average of 567 generated tokens per decision on JevBench and 458 on bev-decision. For Tacit-4B, it added 305 and 187 respectively. github . AnyJev code example . The following example is copied from the AnyJev repository and shows a Tacit decision over customer-service actions. github . from anyjev import Tacit tacit = Tacit.from_pretrained("morriszjm/Tacit-9B") d = tacit.decide( state="Customer: my package was due last Monday and it still has not arrived.", question="What does the customer want?", options=["track_order", "cancel_order", "refund", "change_address"], ) d["answer"] # selected option d["probs"] # {option: probability} d["route"] # "one_forward" or "cot" . For a training-free decision model over an arbitrary open LLM: github . from anyjev import Decider, Question from anyjev.backends.hf import HFBackend d = Decider(HFBackend("Qwen/Qwen3-8B")) # level="L0" by default route = Question.choice( "Which team should handle this?", ["billing", "technical", "sales", "other"], name="route", ) result = d.decide( "My card was charged twice for one order.", [route], )["route"] result.distribution result.level . AnyJev also supports vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp backends. For a stock vLLM server, the client needs only the tokenizer. github . pip install "anyjev[client]" vllm serve morriszjm/Tacit-9B --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 . tacit = Tacit.from_pretrained( "morriszjm/Tacit-9B", engine="server", base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", adaptive=True, ) .

28.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
28.title: Part 5: Calibration
28.content: Why calibration matters . A model can be accurate while still having unreliable probabilities. Calibration measures whether predicted confidence matches observed correctness. For example, if a model assigns approximately 74% positive probability to many movie reviews, then roughly 74% of those reviews should actually be positive for the model to be well calibrated at that confidence level. magazine.sebastianraschka . This distinction is critical for decision systems because the application may use probability thresholds to automate actions: . | Automatically route requests above 0.95 confidence. | Send 0.70 to 0.95 to a cheaper secondary check. | Escalate below 0.70 to a human or reasoning model. | . An accurate but overconfident model will automate too many incorrect decisions. An underconfident model will escalate too much, increasing cost and latency. Expected calibration error . Expected Calibration Error, or ECE, is a common calibration metric. Conceptually, it groups predictions by confidence bucket and compares average predicted confidence with observed accuracy in each bucket: . \[\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_b \frac{n_b}{N} \left| \mathrm{acc}(b) - \mathrm{conf}(b) \right|\] where: . | $b$ indexes confidence bins. | $n_b$ is the number of predictions in bin $b$. | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $\mathrm{acc}(b)$ is observed accuracy in the bin. | $\mathrm{conf}(b)$ is average predicted confidence in the bin. | . Lower ECE indicates better calibration. AnyJev reports ECE reduction from 0.240 with raw logits to 0.184 with L0 on its Qwen3-8B BANKING77 evaluation. github . Temperature scaling . Temperature scaling is a common post-hoc calibration method. It divides logits by a learned positive temperature $T$ before softmax: . $ p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)} $ . where: . | $z_i$ is the logit for candidate $i$. | $T$ is learned on a held-out calibration set. | $T > 1$ generally reduces confidence. | $0 < T < 1$ generally increases confidence. | . Temperature scaling preserves the ordering of logits, so it changes confidence without changing the argmax decision. This general calibration background is added for clarity; it is not a claim about the internal training method of every decision model. magazine.sebastianraschka . Calibration in decision models . Decision models are designed around calibrated confidence. Jev’s documentation describes its probabilities as well calibrated, and the JEV-as-a-Judge paper uses the model’s confidence directly to decide whether to accept a verdict or escalate it to a reasoning judge. magazine.sebastianraschka . However, calibration is dataset- and distribution-dependent. A model calibrated on support-ticket routing may not be calibrated on medical triage, code review, or adversarial text. Production systems should validate thresholds on representative local data before relying on confidence-based automation. arxiv .

29.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
29.title: Part 6: Decision Cascades
29.content: Accept or escalate . A decision cascade uses a fast decision model as the first stage and escalates uncertain or high-stakes cases to a slower reasoning system. Input state | v +----------------------+ | Decision model | Returns probabilities| +----------------------+ | confidence >= threshold |--------------------------------+ | v v Accept decision Escalate to System 2 - reasoning LLM - human reviewer - tool-using agent . This architecture is valuable when most decisions are easy but a minority require deeper reasoning. The fast model handles the bulk of traffic; the expensive path handles only uncertain cases. JEV-as-a-Judge results . The JEV-as-a-Judge paper studies evaluation with JEV as a decision-only judge that returns label probabilities instead of text. Its confidence determines whether to accept the verdict or escalate to a reasoning judge. arxiv . Key reported findings: . | Against 16 generative and reward-model judges, with blinded human adjudication, JEV came within three points of GPT-6 wherever a verdict could be read from the text. | It did so at 0.36% of GPT-6’s fee and with a 0.15-second median latency. | It fell behind where the verdict had to be derived, such as math, code, and logic. | With a threshold frozen in advance, accepting confident verdicts and escalating the rest was 0.9 points more accurate than GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs, at 41% of GPT-6’s fee. | In a pre-specified live test on two new workloads, the cascade matched GPT-6’s accuracy exactly. | Confidence routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose. arxiv | . The practical lesson is that a decision model is strongest when the judgment can be read from the supplied evidence. It is weaker when the correct answer requires deriving a new result through multi-step reasoning.

30.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
30.title: Part 7: Search and Agent Applications
30.content: SearchJev . SearchJev is a fast, calibrated System-1 model for search agents. It separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. arxiv . Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev directly scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. It uses Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions, or SLCD, to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and calibrate confidence. arxiv . SearchDecision-Bench unifies six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. The paper reports: . | SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models. | It achieves 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions. | It reduces average expected calibration error by 41% to 74%. | In dual-system agents on BrowseComp-Plus, active search time improves by 3.7 to 4.7 times. | Answer accuracy improves from 45% to up to 54%. arxiv | . Search-agent decision examples . Typical System-1 decisions in a search agent include: . | Decision | Candidate options | Use of result | . | Relevance | Relevant, not relevant | Filter or retain a document | . | Evidence sufficiency | Sufficient, insufficient | Stop searching or continue | . | Next action | Search, read, refine query, answer | Control the agent loop | . | Query quality | Good, needs refinement | Decide whether to regenerate a query | . These examples illustrate the decision types described by SearchJev; the exact benchmark schema contains six decision types, and the paper should be consulted for the complete task definitions. arxiv . Agent policy and routing . In an agent system, decision models can gate actions before execution: . Agent observes state | v Decision model | +-- safe_action probability high --> execute tool | +-- uncertain or unsafe -----------> ask planner / human | +-- policy violation --------------> block action . The decision layer is especially useful for: . | Selecting a tool or backend. | Checking whether an action is allowed by policy. | Deciding whether retrieved evidence supports an answer. | Triage of incidents, tickets, invoices, or agent traces. | Scoring completed agent runs against a rubric. vllm-sr | .

31.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
31.title: Part 8: Building and Fine-Tuning
31.content: When to fine-tune . A general decision model is attractive when tasks change frequently or labeled data is scarce. A specialized classifier can still be better when: . | The task is narrow and stable. | Latency requirements are extreme. | The label set is fixed. | Large volumes of high-quality labeled data exist. | The cost of maintaining a custom model is acceptable. | . Sebastian Raschka’s analysis frames the trade-off clearly: Jev-like models are more general than task-specific classifiers, while specialized classifiers can be better, faster, and cheaper for a narrow, well-defined problem. magazine.sebastianraschka . SFT workflow . Supervised fine-tuning, or SFT, adapts a decision model to domain-specific states, questions, candidates, and preferred decisions. The Liquid4All cookbook provides SFT notebooks for decision models using both Unsloth and TRL. vllm-sr . A typical workflow is: . 1. Define decision schema - state fields - questions - candidate sets - score rubrics 2. Collect or synthesize examples - state - question - correct option or score level 3. Format for SFT - preserve candidate order policy - include candidate descriptions - retain task instructions 4. Fine-tune - train model and decision head - use validation split for calibration 5. Evaluate - accuracy - calibration error - escalation rate - latency and cost 6. Deploy - serve with vLLM, llama.cpp, or managed endpoint - monitor drift and threshold performance . This workflow is a general engineering reconstruction; the exact data format and training hyperparameters depend on the chosen framework and base model. Unsloth and TRL . Unsloth provides documentation and tooling for training your own decision model, and the Liquid4All cookbook includes notebooks for SFT with both Unsloth and TRL. vllm-sr . | Tool | Role | . | Unsloth | Efficient fine-tuning library and decision-model training guide | . | TRL | Transformer Reinforcement Learning library for training workflows | . | Hugging Face | Model and dataset hosting | . | vLLM | High-throughput serving | . | llama.cpp | Local CPU/GPU inference for supported model formats | . These are infrastructure options; selecting one does not by itself guarantee calibration or accuracy. Evaluation on task-specific held-out data remains necessary.

32.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
32.title: Part 9: Deployment
32.content: Local inference . Decision 1.0 provides weights and local inference code in its model repositories. An HTTP endpoint must be deployed separately if the application uses the System One-compatible HTTP interface. vllm-sr . AnyJev supports several execution modes: . | Mode | Description | . | transformers | In-process Hugging Face Transformers execution | . | vllm | vLLM running in the same process | . | server | Client to a separately running vllm serve endpoint | . | HTTP gateway | AnyJev endpoint in front of an upstream model server | . The AnyJev HTTP gateway listens on 127.0.0.1 and has no authentication of its own, so it should not be exposed directly to untrusted networks without adding authentication and transport security. github . System One request format . Decision 1.0 uses the upstream System One request format: state, model, and named questions. The official TypeSafe Python SDK or an equivalent HTTP request can be used with a SystemOne-compatible deployment. vllm-sr . Install the SDK: . pip install typesafe-sdk . The following Python example is published in the Lux model card and reproduced from the Decision 1.0 announcement. vllm-sr . from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, TypeSafeClient with TypeSafeClient( api_key="YOUR_ENDPOINT_API_KEY", base_url="https://your-decision-endpoint.example", model="Decision-1.0-Lux-9B", ) as client: result = client.system_one( state="Customer reports a duplicate charge and asks for a refund.", questions={ "route": Choice( instructions="Which team should handle this request?", criteria={ "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Product faults", }, ), "refund_requested": Noul( instructions="Did the customer request a refund?" ), }, ) print(result.choices["route"].choice) print(result.nouls["refund_requested"].noul) . The equivalent HTTP request is: vllm-sr . curl -X POST 'https://your-decision-endpoint.example/v1/systemone' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ENDPOINT_API_KEY' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data-raw '{ "model": "Decision-1.0-Lux-9B", "state": "Customer reports a duplicate charge and asks for a refund.", "questions": { "route": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this request?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Product faults" } }, "refund_requested": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the customer request a refund?" } } }' . Deployment checklist . | Define explicit candidate descriptions rather than relying only on short labels. | Set action thresholds from local validation data, not intuition. | Log the full probability distribution, not only the selected option. | Monitor calibration, escalation rate, latency, cost, and drift. | Bound reasoning escalation with a token budget and a share cap. | Keep a human or System-2 path for high-impact or low-confidence decisions. | Test candidate-order sensitivity, especially when using raw logits. | Validate behavior under adversarial, out-of-distribution, and reference-free inputs. github | .

33.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
33.title: Part 10: Comparisons and Trade-Offs
33.content: Decision model versus classifier versus LLM . | Dimension | Task-specific classifier | Decision model | Generative LLM | . | Candidate set | Usually fixed at training time | Supplied at inference time | Can be specified in the prompt | . | Output | Label or score | Typed distribution over candidates | Free-form text | . | Training need | Usually requires task labels | Can be zero-shot, training-free, or fine-tuned | Can be prompted without training | . | Latency | Usually lowest | Low, especially with one-pass readout | Higher when generating text | . | Cost | Low at scale | Low to moderate | Highest for reasoning-heavy paths | . | Generality | Narrow | Broad across decision tasks | Broadest | . | Reasoning depth | Limited | Limited unless escalated | Strongest | . | Calibration | Requires evaluation and post-processing | Core design goal | Often requires additional calibration work | . This comparison combines source claims with general engineering context. The source material specifically emphasizes that Jev-like models occupy a middle ground: more general than a custom classifier, faster and cheaper than using a large generative model for every decision. magazine.sebastianraschka . One-pass readout versus reasoning escalation . | Approach | Latency | Cost | Accuracy potential | When to use | . | Raw logits | Very low | Very low | Sensitive to order and label bias | Prototyping only | . | L0 rotations | Low to moderate | Low | Better order robustness and calibration | Training-free decisions | . | Tacit one-forward | Very low | Low | Strong when model is well trained | High-volume operational decisions | . | Adaptive reasoning escalation | Variable | Higher | Better on uncertain cases | High-stakes or ambiguous decisions | . | Full System-2 reasoning | Highest | Highest | Strongest for derivation-heavy tasks | Planning, math, code, complex logic | . AnyJev’s adaptive mode operationalizes this trade-off by sending only a capped share of low-confidence decisions to reasoning. github .

34.doc: Decision Models (Part1): The Decision Layer for AI Systems
34.title: Part 11: Limitations and Open Questions
34.content: Known limitations . | Derived answers are harder. JEV-as-a-Judge found that decision-only judging falls behind where the verdict must be derived, such as math, code, and logic. arxiv | Adversarial and reference-free evaluation are difficult. Confidence routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose. arxiv | Calibration is not universal. A model calibrated on one distribution may be miscalibrated on another; local threshold validation is necessary. arxiv | Candidate order can matter. Raw label logits can flip answers when options are reordered; AnyJev’s L0 reduces but does not inherently eliminate the need for careful evaluation. github | Escalation costs tokens. AnyJev reports hundreds of additional generated tokens per escalated decision for Tacit-9B and Tacit-4B. github | Benchmark scores are suite-dependent. Decision 1.0’s results use a selected 54-task suite and a weighted overall metric; they should not be generalized as universal superiority. vllm-sr | Open questions remain. AnyJev’s roadmap lists label-free early exit, agent-loop evaluation, additional log-prob backends, and span readout beyond 26 options as areas still under development. github | . Evaluation gaps . Production adoption should evaluate more than headline accuracy: . | Accuracy by decision type and candidate-set size. | ECE and reliability diagrams. | Automation rate at a fixed error budget. | Escalation rate and reasoning-token cost. | Sensitivity to candidate order and paraphrasing. | Out-of-distribution performance. | Latency distributions, including median and p95. | Failure impact by action severity. | .

41.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
41.title: Overview
41.content: Generative large language models (LLMs) operate through autoregressive next-token generation, producing output one token at a time. For deterministic classification, multi-class routing, entity extraction, and structured action selection, this sequential decoding can introduce avoidable latency, memory overhead, and unreliable confidence. Decision models shift this workload away from generative autoregression toward prefill-only, Joint Energy Value (JEV), and energy-based model (EBM) architectures. Instead of generating a label as text, the model scores a supplied candidate set and returns a probability distribution over the candidates. The core decision pattern is: . \[\text{State} + \text{Question} + \text{Candidate Set} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distribution}\] Decision 1.0 expresses this as state + questions + criteria → typed probability distributions, where the application defines the allowed choices and the model evaluates them. vllm-sr . +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Generative Auto-Regressive Paradigm | | Input Prompt -> [ Encoder Prefill ] -> [ Token 1 ] -> [ Token 2 ] ... [ END ] | (Sequential O(N) generation loops) | | Latency: High (100 ms - 2,000 ms) | Memory: KV-cache bound | Calibration: Often poor without additional work | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ VS +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Decision Model (JEV) Paradigm | | Input Prompt + Candidate Set -> [ Prefill Encoder ] -> [ Joint Energy Head ] | (Single forward pass) | | Latency: Low, especially for short contexts | Memory: No generated-token KV-cache growth | Calibration: Designed for typed probability outputs | +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ . The latency, memory, and calibration characteristics shown above are conceptual representations of the two paradigms. Actual results depend on model size, sequence length, batch size, hardware, serving engine, and candidate-set size.

42.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
42.title: Part 1: Foundations of Decision Models vs. Generative LLMs
42.content: Traditional generative LLMs often evaluate class probabilities by predicting text tokens, such as generating "Yes", "No", or a JSON object. This introduces engineering and statistical challenges in production systems: . | The model may emit malformed JSON or an invalid class name. | The output must be parsed and validated. | Label order can affect next-token logits. | Confidence from generated text is often poorly calibrated. | Each generated token adds sequential decoding work. | . By contrast, a decision model receives the candidate options directly and scores them in context. Decision 1.0 evaluates each supplied candidate against the evidence and question, returning probabilities rather than generated text. vllm-sr .

43.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
43.title: Computational and architectural comparison
43.content: | Dimension | Generative autoregressive LLMs | Prefill-only / decision models (JEV) | . | Decoding complexity | $O(N)$ sequential autoregressive loops | $O(1)$ single-pass parallel prefill | . | Typical inference latency | Tens to thousands of milliseconds | Low, especially for short contexts | . | KV-cache memory overhead | Grows with generated sequence length | No generated-token KV-cache growth | . | Probabilistic calibration | Often overconfident without calibration work | Designed for typed probability outputs | . | Generative hallucination | Possible syntax errors or invalid classes | Hard-bounded candidate scoring | . | Throughput bottleneck | Often memory-bandwidth bound during decoding | Compute-bound tensor operations during prefill | . | Serving framework | Autoregressive vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, PagedAttention | Prefill-optimized runners, including vLLM and llama.cpp | . The exact latency and throughput depend on the model, context length, batch size, and hardware. The important structural distinction is that decision models avoid generating decision text token by token. vllm-sr .

44.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
44.title: Computational complexity and FLOP breakdown
44.content: For a sequence length $L$, hidden dimension $D$, and $M$ transformer layers, an autoregressive model generating $T$ output tokens requires floating-point operations that scale approximately as: . \[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{generative}} \approx 2 \cdot M \cdot (L \cdot D^2 + T \cdot L \cdot D + T \cdot D^2)\] A prefill-only decision model evaluates the target decision directly over the input sequence without generating additional text, so $T = 0$. The approximate FLOP count reduces to: . \[\text{FLOPs}_{\text{decision}} \approx 2 \cdot M \cdot L \cdot D^2\] This is a simplified approximation. It highlights the main source of savings—removing generated tokens—but does not capture all implementation-specific costs, such as attention overhead, candidate scoring, batching, and memory movement. By removing token-generation loops, serving engines avoid repeated memory-bandwidth work associated with decoding each new token. SearchJev reports that its decision model achieves 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions than same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models on SearchDecision-Bench. arxiv .

45.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
45.title: Part 2: Joint Energy Value (JEV) Mathematical Formulation
45.content: Joint Energy Value (JEV) frameworks ground classification and structured decision-making in energy-based model (EBM) theory. Instead of directly modeling a conditional probability distribution $P(Y \mid X)$ with a simple linear classification head over context $X$, a JEV model assigns a scalar energy $E(X, Y)$ to the joint space of input context $X$ and candidate action or class $Y$. User Context (X) ----+ +---> [ Joint Energy Model E(X, Y) ] ---> Scalar Energy E_i Candidate Class (Y_i)-+ .

46.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
46.title: JEV probability derivation
46.content: Let $X \in \mathcal{X}$ be the input feature space, such as a query, user profile, or document context. Let $Y \in \mathcal{Y} = {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_C}$ be the set of $C$ candidate decisions. The joint probability density $P(X, Y)$ can be parameterized using a Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution: . \[P(X, Y) = \frac{\exp\left( -E(X, Y) / T \right)}{Z}\] where: . | $E(X, Y)$ is the joint energy of context $X$ and candidate $Y$. | $T$ is a temperature parameter. | $Z$ is the partition function. | . The partition function integrates over the configuration space: . \[Z = \sum_{y' \in \mathcal{Y}} \int_{\mathcal{X}} \exp\left( -E(x', y') / T \right) \, dx'\] By marginalizing over $X$, the conditional class probability $P(Y = y_i \mid X)$ cancels the intractable partition function: . \[P(Y = y_i \mid X) = \frac{P(X, Y = y_i)} {\sum_{j=1}^{C} P(X, Y = y_j)} = \frac{\exp\left( -E(X, y_i) / T \right)} {\sum_{j=1}^{C} \exp\left( -E(X, y_j) / T \right)}\] In practice, the model computes energies or logits for the supplied candidates and normalizes them over that candidate set. Decision 1.0 follows this general pattern: it scores the candidates provided in the request and returns their probabilities. vllm-sr .

47.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
47.title: Unconditional marginal energy and OOD detection
47.content: The marginal energy $E(X)$ of input context $X$ is obtained by aggregating energy over all candidate decisions: . \[E(X) = -T \cdot \log \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} \exp\left( \frac{-E(X, y)}{T} \right)\] This marginal energy can be used as an explicit signal for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, intent validation, and retrieval-quality checks. Unconditional Marginal Energy E(X) | +-----------------------+-----------------------+ | Low marginal energy High marginal energy E(X) < threshold E(X) > threshold | v v [ In-distribution query ] [ Out-of-distribution query ] [ Proceed to decision ] [ Fallback / rejection mode ] . Interpretation: . | Low marginal energy: the input is relatively well supported by the candidate space. | High marginal energy: the input may not match any valid candidate, suggesting an OOD input, unsupported context, or invalid request. | . This is a useful design pattern, but it requires empirical threshold selection on representative validation data. A high-energy input is not automatically a hallucination; it may simply be a valid request outside the trained candidate distribution.

48.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
48.title: Part 3: AnyJev, SearchJEV, and Specialized Decision Architectures
48.content: Modern open-weight decision models adopt different architectural approaches depending on deployment constraints, such as e-commerce search, named-entity recognition, RAG routing, and agent action selection. Decision Model Variants | +--------------------------------+--------------------------------+ | | [ AnyJev Architecture ] [ SearchJEV Architecture ] [ GLiNER 2.5 / GLIDE ] - Universal decision readout - Search-state decisions - Entity extraction - Rotation-based L0 readout - Dual-system search agents - Reasoning decision model - Self-distilled Tacit models - Calibrated confidence - Structured extraction .

49.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
49.title: AnyJev: universal decision readout
49.content: AnyJev turns an LLM into a Jev-style decision model. It returns typed decisions and probabilities over supplied options without parsing generated text. github . AnyJev provides two paths: . | Path | Training requirement | Mechanism | . | Training-free Decider | No training, no labels | Reads typed decisions from any open causal LLM | . | Self-distilled Tacit | Uses Tacit checkpoints | One forward pass per decision, with optional adaptive reasoning escalation | . A raw next-token logit readout can change its answer when options are reordered and can carry a preference for particular label strings. AnyJev’s L0 readout averages position bias over rotations of the options and divides out the label prior. github . A conceptual energy-style formulation for a candidate $y_i$ is: . \[E(X, Y = y_i) = -\mathbf{w}_{y_i}^{T} \cdot \text{Pooling}\left( \text{Transformer}\left([X ; y_i]\right) \right)\] where: . | $X$ is the input state. | $y_i$ is a candidate option. | $\mathbf{w}_{y_i}$ is a learnable projection vector for that candidate. | $\text{Pooling}$ produces a fixed-size representation from the transformer output. | . This equation is an illustrative formulation of a pooled candidate-scoring head. It is not a claim that every AnyJev implementation uses this exact parameterization.

50.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
50.title: SearchJEV: low-latency search decisions
50.content: SearchJev is a fast, calibrated System-1 model for search agents. It separates short search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev directly scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. arxiv . A conceptual two-tower formulation for query-product scoring is: . \[E(\text{Query}, \text{Product}_i) = -\left( \phi(\text{Query})^{T} \psi(\text{Product}_i) \right) + b_i\] where: . | $\phi$ is a query encoder. | $\psi$ is a product encoder. | $b_i$ is an item-specific bias term, potentially reflecting popularity or prior click-through rate. | . Query context ---> [ Query encoder phi ] ---> Vector u \ +--> Dot product + bias ---> E(Q, P_i) Product data ---> [ Product encoder psi ] ---> Vector v / . This two-tower structure is a common retrieval and reranking design. SearchJev’s published contribution is specifically its use of Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD), its SearchDecision-Bench benchmark, and its dual-system search-agent evaluation. arxiv .

51.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
51.title: Contrastive learning for decision models
51.content: Contrastive Language Models for decisions, such as Contrastive-LM/CLM-v0.1-8B, can use InfoNCE-style losses over joint energy states. Positive query-decision pairs are pushed toward lower energy, while negative candidates receive higher energy. \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{ \exp\left( -E(X, Y^+) / T \right) }{ \exp\left( -E(X, Y^+) / T \right) + \sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp\left( -E(X, Y_j^-) / T \right) }\] where: . | $Y^+$ is the positive candidate. | $Y_j^-$ are negative candidates. | $K$ is the number of negatives. | $T$ is a temperature parameter. | . This is a standard contrastive-learning formulation added for technical context. The exact loss used by a particular CLM implementation should be verified against its repository and model card.

52.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
52.title: Part 4: Probabilistic Calibration and Overconfidence Analysis
52.content: A common failure mode of autoregressive LLM classifiers is overconfidence: assigning very high softmax probability to incorrect predictions. Decision models address this by making calibrated probability outputs a first-class part of the interface.

53.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
53.title: Expected Calibration Error
53.content: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures the alignment between predicted confidence $\hat{p}$ and observed accuracy across $B$ confidence bins $I_b$: . \[\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{|I_b|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(I_b) - \text{conf}(I_b) \right|\] where: . | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $I_b$ is a confidence bin. | $\text{acc}(I_b)$ is observed accuracy within the bin. | $\text{conf}(I_b)$ is average predicted confidence within the bin. | . \[\text{acc}(I_b) = \frac{1}{|I_b|} \sum_{i \in I_b} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i = y_i), \qquad \text{conf}(I_b) = \frac{1}{|I_b|} \sum_{i \in I_b} \hat{p}_i\] Lower ECE indicates better calibration. Perfect calibration (ECE = 0.0) Overconfident model (high ECE) Accuracy Accuracy 1.0 | / 1.0 | / | / | / . (Actual accuracy) 0.5 | / 0.5 | / . | / | /. <-- Large gap 0.0 +------------ 0.0 +------------ 0.0 0.5 1.0 Confidence 0.0 0.5 1.0 Confidence .
