56.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
56.title: Part 5: Serving Infrastructure and Prefill-Only Optimizations
56.content: Because decision models eliminate autoregressive decoding loops, traditional serving configurations can allocate KV-cache memory that is never used for generated tokens. Standard vLLM pipeline: Input -> [ Prefill phase ] -> [ Allocate KV-cache ] -> [ Decode loop steps 1..N ] (Unnecessary for decision models) Prefill-only vLLM-SR / llama.cpp serving pipeline: Input -> [ Parallel prefill compute ] -> [ Energy scoring head ] -> Return result (Single pass) .

57.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
57.title: Serving optimization strategies
57.content: . | Avoid unnecessary KV-cache allocation. For prefill-only decision workloads, configure the serving engine to avoid retaining KV-cache state for generated tokens that will never be produced. | Use dynamic tensor-core batching. Group many classification requests into large parallel prefill matrix multiplications. | Quantize for edge deployment. GGUF quantized models, such as Q4_K_M or Q8_0, can run through llama.cpp on CPU or edge hardware, subject to accuracy and latency validation. | Batch independent questions. Decision 1.0’s Kai and Lex native Python API accepts up to 128 independent requests and 512 total decisions per local SDK batch submission. The runtime groups work into physical batches; 512 describes submission capacity, not simultaneous forward passes or measured throughput. vllm-sr | Separate candidate scoring from generation. Score all candidates for a question in a single forward pass where the architecture supports it, as Decision 1.0’s Lux model does. vllm-sr | . A simplified batched scoring operation is: . \[\mathbf{Y}_{\text{logits}} = \mathbf{X}_{\text{prefill embeddings}} \cdot \mathbf{W}_{\text{energy head}}^{T}\] where: . | $\mathbf{X}_{\text{prefill embeddings}}$ contains pooled prefill representations. | $\mathbf{W}_{\text{energy head}}$ contains candidate projection weights. | $\mathbf{Y}_{\text{logits}}$ contains raw scores for each candidate. | . Actual serving performance requires measuring p50, p95, and p99 latency under realistic batch sizes and context lengths.

58.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
58.title: Part 6: Training and Fine-Tuning Decision Models with Unsloth and TRL
58.content: Fine-tuning a decoder model, such as Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen-2.5-0.5B, into a decision model generally involves replacing standard causal language-modeling loss with supervised classification loss over pooled hidden states or candidate energy scores. Input sequence [X] | v [ Llama / Qwen backbone ] | v [ Pooled last-token hidden state ] | v [ Energy projection layer ] | v Cross-entropy loss versus target label . This is a supervised classification approach. It differs from AnyJev’s self-distillation approach, in which a Tacit model learns to produce in one forward pass the answers it reaches when it reasons, without human labels or a separate teacher model. github .

59.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
59.title: Fine-tuning pipeline with Unsloth and PyTorch
59.content: The following script is an illustrative implementation. It loads a lightweight base backbone, attaches a classification head, and fine-tunes it with Unsloth. It is not copied from the official Unsloth or Liquid4All decision-model notebooks and should be adapted to the target data schema and model. import torch from torch import nn from unsloth import FastLanguageModel from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments from datasets import Dataset # 1. Configuration and model loading max_seq_length = 2048 dtype = None # Auto-detect Float16 or BFloat16 load_in_4bit = True model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct", max_seq_length=max_seq_length, dtype=dtype, load_in_4bit=load_in_4bit, ) # 2. Add LoRA adapters model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, target_modules=[ "q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj", ], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=3407, ) # 3. Define a custom decision head wrapper class JEVDecisionModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, base_model, num_classes, hidden_dim): super().__init__() self.base_model = base_model self.energy_head = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, num_classes, bias=False) def forward(self, input_ids, attention_mask, labels=None): outputs = self.base_model( input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, output_hidden_states=True, ) # Use the final-token representation as the pooled decision state. last_hidden_state = outputs.hidden_states[-1][:, -1, :] # Treat logits as negative energies: E(X, Y) = -logits. logits = self.energy_head(last_hidden_state) loss = None if labels is not None: loss_fct = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() loss = loss_fct(logits, labels) return {"loss": loss, "logits": logits} # 4. Prepare a small illustrative dataset train_data = { "text": [ "Category: Electronics | Query: Wireless noise canceling headphones", "Category: Clothing | Query: Cotton summer t-shirt blue", "Category: Books | Query: Introduction to quantum computing algorithm", ], "label": [0, 1, 2], # 0: Electronics, 1: Clothing, 2: Books } def tokenize_function(examples): tokens = tokenizer( examples["text"], padding="max_length", max_length=128, truncation=True, ) tokens["labels"] = examples["label"] return tokens dataset = Dataset.from_dict(train_data) tokenized_dataset = dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True) # 5. Configure training training_args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./jev_decision_model_checkpoints", per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=2, warmup_steps=5, max_steps=30, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=not torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), bf16=torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), logging_steps=1, optim="adamw_8bit", weight_decay=0.01, lr_scheduler_type="linear", seed=3407, ) # 6. Instantiate the wrapper and trainer wrapped_model = JEVDecisionModel( base_model=model, num_classes=3, hidden_dim=model.config.hidden_size, ) trainer = Trainer( model=wrapped_model, args=training_args, train_dataset=tokenized_dataset, ) # 7. Train trainer.train() . For production training, use a sufficiently large and representative labeled dataset, reserve a held-out validation split, and evaluate accuracy, calibration, latency, and escalation behavior—not training loss alone.

64.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
64.title: Dynamic candidate spaces
64.content: Standard JEV-style models require a predefined candidate set $\mathcal{Y}$. Evaluating millions of dynamic candidates in a single pass is usually impractical. A common hybrid approach is: . Large candidate universe | v [ Bi-encoder / vector search prefilter ] | v [ Top-K candidate set ] | v [ Decision model scores top-K candidates ] | v [ Typed probability distribution ] . This combines the recall of vector search with the calibrated scoring of a decision model.

65.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
65.title: Context-window scaling
65.content: Prefill-only execution removes autoregressive decoding, but it does not remove the cost of processing a long input. For very long contexts, attention can still incur substantial compute and memory cost during the initial prefill phase. For standard full attention, prefill attention cost scales approximately as: . \[O(L^2)\] where $L$ is the sequence length. Hybrid architectures, sparse attention, sliding-window attention, and efficient sequence mixers can reduce this cost, but their effectiveness depends on the workload.

66.doc: Decision Models & Joint Energy Value (JEV) Architectures (Part 2): Technical Reference Guide
66.title: Multi-step reasoning
66.content: Complex mathematical logic, multi-step planning, and chain-of-thought reasoning cannot always be compressed into a single-pass prefill. Hybrid “thinking” decision models, such as Fastino GLIDE, are one approach to combining fast decision readouts with selective reasoning. AnyJev takes a related approach with adaptive escalation: low-confidence Tacit decisions can be sent to the model’s own reasoning, subject to a configured cap. At the default settings, at most 20% of the last 1,000 decisions escalate, and each escalated decision has a reasoning budget of 8,192 tokens. github .

67.title: Final Technical Takeaways
67.content: . | Paradigm shift: Decision models eliminate sequential token-generation loops for structured decisions, scoring supplied candidates through a prefill-oriented decision path. | Efficiency: Removing generated-token decoding avoids KV-cache growth during decision generation and can substantially reduce latency; SearchJev reports 5.2 to 5.3 times faster decisions than same-size autoregressive models on its benchmark. arxiv | Calibration: JEV-style probability outputs make confidence usable for policy thresholds. AnyJev’s L0 readout reduces ECE from 0.240 to 0.184 and increases the share of decisions automatable at 5% error or less from 7.7% to 46.3% without labels. github | OOD safety: Marginal energy $E(X)$ provides a mathematical signal for detecting unsupported inputs, invalid agent tool calls, and out-of-distribution queries, subject to empirical threshold calibration. | Main trade-off: Single-pass decision models are fast and inexpensive, but derivation-heavy tasks still require System-2 reasoning, planning, or human escalation. arxiv | Engineering implication: Use decision models as a programmable control layer between understanding and action: define candidate sets explicitly, return calibrated distributions, automate only within validated confidence thresholds, and escalate uncertain or high-impact cases. vllm-sr | .

69.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
69.title: Decision Models for Query Understanding: A Calibrated Decision Layer for Search and AI Systems
69.content: References: . | AnyJev: Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model | SearchJev: A Fast and Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents | GLiNER-2.5-Decide: Open-weight structured decision model | Decision 1.0: Open Decision Foundation Models | . Search systems often need to make many small decisions before they can retrieve anything useful: Did the user misspell an artist name? Is this a song title or a podcast name? Should the query be rewritten? Is there enough evidence to proceed? Should the system ask a larger model for help? . A common approach is to send the query to a generative LLM and ask it to return JSON. That works, but it turns a bounded decision problem into an open-ended text-generation problem. The model may produce malformed JSON, invent an entity type, change its answer when options are reordered, or assign high confidence to an incorrect interpretation. Decision models offer a different contract: . \[\text{Query} + \text{Context} + \text{Candidate Set} \rightarrow \text{Typed probability distribution}\] Instead of generating an answer, the model scores supplied candidates and returns calibrated probabilities. This makes query understanding faster, more constrained, and easier to operate in production. AnyJev describes this pattern as typed decisions with real probabilities: a choice among options, a yes/no decision, or an ordinal score, read from a model’s distribution in one prefill. SearchJev applies the same idea to search agents, separating fast System-1 decisions from slower System-2 reasoning and generation. github .

70.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
70.title: The core intuition
70.content: Most query-understanding systems do not need to generate language. They need to choose among possibilities. Given a noisy query such as: . tailor swift songs . the system must decide: . | Is this a spelling mistake? | Should it become taylor swift songs? | Is taylor swift an artist, song, album, or something else? | Is songs a media-type indicator? | Should the system search the catalog directly, reformulate the query, or escalate? | . A generative model can answer these questions by writing JSON. A decision model answers them by scoring bounded alternatives: . Raw query: tailor swift songs Correction candidates: - KEEP_ORIGINAL 0.02 - taylor swift songs 0.94 - tailor swift song 0.02 - taylor swift music 0.02 Interpretation candidates: - ArtistName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.96 - SongName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.03 - AlbumName:taylor swift + MediaType:SONG 0.01 . The application—not the model—then decides what to do with those probabilities. For example, it may automatically route high-confidence queries, retrieve catalog candidates for medium-confidence queries, and escalate low-confidence queries. This is the central idea: the decision model chooses; the surrounding system acts.

71.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
71.title: Why not just prompt an LLM?
71.content: A generative LLM is flexible, but flexibility has a cost. | Concern | Generative JSON output | Decision-model output | . | Output format | Text that must be parsed and validated | Typed, schema-bounded decisions | . | Invalid answers | Possible invented fields or class names | Structurally constrained | . | Latency | Grows with generated tokens | Can score candidates in one pass | . | Confidence | Often poorly calibrated | Designed for thresholdable probabilities | . | Candidate-order sensitivity | Can change with option order | Can be reduced with rotation or calibration methods | . | Cost | Higher for reasoning-heavy paths | Lower for high-volume decisions | . | Best use | Open-ended reasoning and generation | Routing, classification, extraction, gating | . AnyJev’s documentation highlights a specific failure mode of raw LLM label logits: answers can flip when the order of options changes. Its rotation-based readout reduces order sensitivity and improves calibration without requiring labels. github . That matters because production systems often use confidence thresholds: . | Automatically route queries above 0.90 confidence. | Retrieve more evidence between 0.70 and 0.90. | Escalate below 0.70. | . An accurate but overconfident model will automate too many mistakes. An underconfident model will escalate too much, increasing latency and cost.

72.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
72.title: A factored decision graph
72.content: A naive design might try to enumerate every spelling correction and every possible interpretation: . \[\text{Candidates} = M \times N\] where $M$ is the number of spelling corrections and $N$ is the number of interpretations. That becomes expensive quickly. If a query has three uncertain tokens, each with five corrections, and each correction has ten interpretations, the system would consider: . \[5^3 \times 10 = 1{,}250\] paths. A better design factors the decision: . \[P(C, R, I, S \mid X, U, K) = P(C \mid X, U, K) \cdot P(R \mid X, C, U, K) \cdot P(I \mid X, C, R, U, K) \cdot P(S \mid X, C, R, I, U, K)\] where: . | $X$ is the raw query. | $C$ is the selected correction. | $R$ is the reformulation strategy or rewritten query. | $I$ is the selected interpretation. | $S$ is the slot assignment. | $U$ is user and session context. | $K$ is catalog or retrieval context. | . Raw query | v Correction candidates | v Decision model: select correction | v Reformulation candidates | v Decision model: select reformulation | v Interpretation candidates | v Decision model: select interpretation | v Slot spans, types, canonical values | v Structured query understanding . At each stage, retain only the top-$k$ candidates. This converts an exponential search into a bounded beam search.

73.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
73.title: What a decision model should own
73.content: A decision model is excellent at selection among bounded alternatives. | Task | Decision-model role | . | Spelling correction | Choose among correction candidates | . | Intent detection | Choose music, podcast, audiobook, or unknown | . | Slot detection | Predict token-level spans | . | Slot typing | Choose among entity types | . | Canonicalization | Choose among closed vocabularies | . | Language detection | Choose among language codes | . | Interpretation selection | Choose among candidate interpretations | . | Reformulation | Choose a rewrite strategy or candidate rewrite | . | Autocomplete | Rank candidate completions | . | RAG grounding | Decide whether retrieval is needed and whether evidence is sufficient | . | Escalation | Decide whether a larger reasoner is needed | . It is less suitable for open-ended creation. | Task | Better approach | . | Generate every possible spelling correction | Edit-distance, phonetic, embedding, or catalog index | . | Generate every possible rewrite | Template rewriter or small generator | . | Generate arbitrary autocomplete text | Language-model generator plus decision reranker | . | Resolve a brand-new entity | Fresh catalog retrieval | . | Perform multi-hop reasoning | Larger reasoner or agent | . The practical rule is simple: . Use retrieval or a small generator to create candidates. Use a decision model to score, select, calibrate, and route them.

74.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
74.title: A practical architecture
74.content: +---------------------------+ User query ------------->| Input normalization | Voice transcript ------> | - lowercase | Locale / market -------->| - punctuation cleanup | Session context -------> | - privacy filtering | +-------------+-------------+ | v +-----------------------------------+ | Candidate generators | | - spelling candidates | - phonetic candidates | - catalog candidates | - autocomplete candidates | - reformulation candidates | - RAG retrieval candidates | +-----------------+-----------------+ | v +-----------------------------------+ | Decision model | | - correction selection | - interpretation selection | - slot spans and types | - canonical values | - language | - ambiguity | - reformulation strategy | - autocomplete selection | - RAG grounding decision | +-----------------+-----------------+ | +-----------------+-----------------+ | v v +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | High-confidence path | Low-confidence path | Return structured | Retrieve, reason, | query understanding | or escalate | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ . This is one decision model in the deployment sense: one encoder, one set of weights, one service. Internally, it has multiple decision heads. Query + context + candidates | +-----------------------+ | Shared encoder | +-----------+-----------+ | +-----------+-----------+-------+-------+-------------+-----------+ | | | v v v v v v Correction Intent and Span and Canonical Language Ambiguity / selection language slot-type value head head routing head head heads head .

75.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
75.title: Spelling correction without overcorrection
75.content: Spelling correction should never blindly change the user’s query. Always include a KEEP_ORIGINAL candidate. Raw query: tailor swift songs Candidates: 0. KEEP_ORIGINAL 1. taylor swift songs 2. tailor swift song 3. taylor swift music . The decision model returns: . { "KEEP_ORIGINAL": 0.02, "taylor swift songs": 0.94, "tailor swift song": 0.02, "taylor swift music": 0.02 } . Candidate generators can include: . | Edit-distance indexes. | Phonetic indexes. | Catalog n-gram indexes. | Embedding retrievers. | Query-log correction indexes. | Language-specific normalizers. | Transliteration variant generators. | ASR-error normalizers. | . For voice interfaces, leading commands such as play, put on, and find me should usually be treated as command or stopword tokens, not as content entities.

76.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
76.title: Handling multiple interpretations
76.content: Some queries are genuinely ambiguous. Query: drake . This could mean: . | An artist. | A song. | A podcast. | An album. | . The correct behavior depends on context. A decision model can score candidate interpretations using catalog data, user history, market, and session signals. Candidate interpretations: 1. ArtistName:drake 0.82 2. SongName:drake 0.09 3. ProgramName:drake 0.06 4. AlbumName:drake 0.03 . Confidence should measure whether the slot type is correct, not whether the exact entity is known. For example, jolene may match songs by multiple artists, but it is still confidently a song title. By contrast, the mill could be a song, artist, album, or podcast, so the slot type itself may be uncertain. This distinction prevents a common failure mode: treating ambiguity about which entity as though it were ambiguity about what kind of thing the user wants.

77.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
77.title: Autocomplete as a decision problem
77.content: Autocomplete has two distinct problems: . | Task | Input | Output | Approach | . | Completion selection | Prefix plus candidate completions | Ranked completions | Decision model | . | Completion generation | Prefix only | Possible continuations | Generator plus decision reranker | . For a prefix such as calm hindi, a candidate generator might produce: . - calm hindi songs - calm hindi romantic songs - calm hindi playlist - calm hindi 90s songs . The decision model then ranks them: . calm hindi songs 0.58 calm hindi romantic songs 0.22 calm hindi playlist 0.12 calm hindi 90s songs 0.08 . This keeps autocomplete fast and controllable. The generator explores; the decision model chooses.

78.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
78.title: RAG grounding
78.content: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is often discussed as a way to give a model current facts. In query understanding, it has a narrower and more useful role: grounding an interpretation in authoritative context. Useful retrieval sources include: . | Catalog metadata. | Entity aliases. | User library and preferences. | Recent releases. | Regional availability. | Knowledge-graph relationships. | Optional web evidence. | . The decision model should decide: . Does this query need retrieval? Which retrieval source should be used? Is the retrieved evidence sufficient? Which candidate entity best resolves the query? Should the system escalate? . Corrected query | v Grounding decision model | +-- no retrieval needed --> return interpretation | +-- retrieval needed -----> retrieve candidates | v Grounded decision model | +-- sufficient --> return interpretation | +-- insufficient -> escalate . Latency matters here. Catalog and user-library retrieval can often fit a low-latency budget. Web retrieval usually cannot. | Path | Typical latency | . | No retrieval | 5–20 ms | . | Local catalog retrieval | 10–25 ms | . | User-library retrieval | 10–30 ms | . | Knowledge-graph retrieval | 20–50 ms | . | Web retrieval | Hundreds of milliseconds or more | . Therefore, web retrieval belongs offline, in an escalation path, or in asynchronous enrichment—not in the primary sub-30 ms path.

79.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
79.title: Calibration is the product
79.content: A decision model’s most valuable output is often not the selected label. It is the probability distribution. Expected Calibration Error, or ECE, measures whether predicted confidence matches observed accuracy: . \[\text{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{|I_b|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(I_b) - \text{conf}(I_b) \right|\] where: . | $I_b$ is a confidence bin. | $N$ is the total number of predictions. | $\text{acc}(I_b)$ is observed accuracy in the bin. | $\text{conf}(I_b)$ is average predicted confidence in the bin. | . Lower ECE means the model’s confidence is more trustworthy. AnyJev reports that its rotation-based readout reduced order-flip rate from 0.230 to 0.073 and improved calibration error from 0.240 to 0.095 in its published README example. The exact numbers depend on the model, dataset, and evaluation setup, but the lesson generalizes: calibration should be measured and improved directly, not treated as an afterthought. github .

80.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
80.title: When to escalate
80.content: A small decision model should not pretend to know everything. Escalate when: . | The query is highly ambiguous. | The language or script is rare. | The entity is new and absent from catalog features. | The query requires multi-hop reasoning. | The query is adversarial or safety-sensitive. | Confidence falls below a validated threshold. | . AnyJev’s Tacit models illustrate a bounded escalation design: they answer typed decisions in one forward pass, but with adaptive mode enabled, a capped share of low-confidence decisions can be sent to the model’s own reasoning. The escalation is reported and constrained by configuration such as tau, max_cot_share, and cot_window. Decision model | +-- high confidence --> return structured decision | +-- low confidence ---> retrieval, reasoner, or human review . The escalation path should have its own latency objective, cost budget, and monitoring. It should not silently violate the primary path’s service-level objective.

81.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
81.title: Can a small model match a large model?
81.content: For constrained query understanding, often yes—on the common query distribution. A 300M-parameter decision model can match or exceed a 7B generative model when: . | The label schema is fixed. | Training data is diverse and grounded in real usage. | The catalog provides current entity resolution. | Queries are short or medium length. | The system is regularly calibrated and refreshed. | . It will usually lose when: . | The query requires broad world knowledge. | The entity is new and absent from retrieval features. | The language is rare or unsupported. | The query requires multi-step reasoning. | The query is adversarial or intentionally ambiguous. | . The right goal is not “make a small model universally equal to a 7B model.” The right goal is: . Make the small model excellent on high-volume, well-understood queries, and escalate the minority that genuinely need more capacity.

82.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
82.title: Production lessons
82.content: . | Separate selection from generation. Decision models select; retrievers and generators create. | Factor the decision space. Do not enumerate every correction-interpretation pair. | Always include a no-change option. This prevents overcorrection. | Use calibrated probabilities for policy. Confidence thresholds should be learned from validation data. | Ground against fresh context. The model interprets; the catalog resolves current facts. | Personalize carefully. User history should disambiguate, not override explicit intent. | Escalate deliberately. Use a bounded reasoning path for uncertainty, not as a default. | Measure calibration in production. Accuracy alone is insufficient for automated decision systems. | .

83.doc: Decision Models for Query Understanding in Search and AI Systems
83.title: Final takeaways
83.content: . | Central mechanism: A decision model maps a query, context, and candidate set to typed probability distributions. | Main architectural insight: Query understanding is mostly a bounded selection problem, not an open-ended generation problem. | Best system shape: Candidate generators create options; a decision model scores, selects, calibrates, and routes. | Key trade-off: A small decision model gives low latency and reliable structure; a larger reasoner gives broader coverage for rare or difficult cases. | Main limitation: A decision model cannot efficiently create an unbounded candidate space or resolve every new entity without retrieval. | Broader implication: Build AI systems as calibrated decision graphs, with fast System-1 decisions handling volume and slower System-2 reasoning reserved for genuine uncertainty. github | .

85.title: Building GPT from Scratch
85.content: Reference Lecture by Andrej Karpathy: YouTube Link .

86.title: 1. Introduction & Core Philosophy
86.content: . | The Core Premise: At its fundamental level, a Large Language Model (LLM) is an auto-complete system. Given a sequence of input text (context), it predicts the probability distribution of the next token. | The Transformer Backbone: Modern LLMs rely entirely on the Transformer architecture introduced in “Attention Is All You Need”, which uses self-attention mechanisms to dynamically weigh relationships between tokens across sequences. | Scope of Implementation: While massive models like ChatGPT incorporate petabytes of web data, multi-stage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), building a foundational GPT from scratch can be demonstrated locally on a tiny dataset (e.g., Shakespeare’s works, $\approx 1\text{MB}$) to understand every tensor operation under the hood. | .

87.title: 2. Reading, Exploring, and Preparing Data
87.content: Before modeling, raw text must be ingested, inspected, and split into training and validation subsets to prevent memorization. 2.1. Ingesting Text Data . Using Python to read raw text: . with open("input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f: text = f.read() # Extract all unique characters to form the vocabulary chars = sorted(list(set(text))) vocab_size = len(chars) print(f"Vocab size: {vocab_size}") . 2.2. Character-Level vs. Sub-Word Tokenization . | Character-Level Tokenization: Used in educational builds (like nanoGPT on Shakespeare) where the vocabulary consists of individual characters (letters, punctuation, numbers). | Sub-Word Tokenization (BPE / SentencePiece): Modern production models (GPT-2/3/4, Llama) use Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) via libraries like tiktoken to group frequent character n-grams into single tokens, shrinking sequence lengths and improving efficiency. | . # Character mapping dictionaries stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(chars)} itos = {i: ch for i, ch in enumerate(chars)} encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s] # String to integer list decode = lambda l: "".join([itos[i] for i in l]) # Integer list to string . 2.3. Train / Validation Split . To verify that the model generalizes rather than merely memorizing the training corpus, the dataset is tokenized into a PyTorch tensor and split (typically 90% train, 10% validation): . import torch data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long) n = int(0.9 * len(data)) train_data = data[:n] val_data = data[n:] . 2.4. Batching and Data Loaders . During training, the model doesn’t process the entire text at once. Instead, it samples random chunks of length block_size (context window) across batches (batch_size): . torch.manual_seed(1337) batch_size = 4 block_size = 8 # maximum context length for predictions def get_batch(split): data = train_data if split == "train" else val_data # Generate random starting indices for batch chunks ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,)) x = torch.stack([data[i : i + block_size] for i in ix]) y = torch.stack([data[i + 1 : i + block_size + 1] for i in ix]) return x, y .

88.title: 3. The Baseline: Bigram Language Model
88.content: As a starting point, Karpathy implements a simple Bigram Language Model where each token prediction depends only on the immediately preceding single token. 3.1. PyTorch Module Structure . import torch.nn as nn from torch.nn import functional as F class BigramLanguageModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size): super().__init__() # Each token reads off the logits for the next token from a lookup table self.token_embedding_table = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, vocab_size) def forward(self, idx, targets=None): # idx and targets are (B, T) tensors of integers logits = self.token_embedding_table(idx) # (B, T, C) -> Batch, Time, Channels if targets is None: loss = None else: B, T, C = logits.shape logits_flat = logits.view(B * T, C) targets_flat = targets.view(B * T) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits_flat, targets_flat) return logits, loss def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens): for _ in range(max_new_tokens): logits, loss = self(idx) # Focus only on the last time step logits = logits[:, -1, :] # becomes (B, C) probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1) # (B, C) idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1) # (B, 1) idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1) # (B, T+1) return idx .

89.title: 4. The Crux: Building Self-Attention Step-by-Step
89.content: The central conceptual breakthrough of the lecture is demonstrating how context aggregation evolves from naive averaging to optimized matrix multiplication. 4.1. Version 1: Naive For-Loops (Averaging Past Context) . To compute the representation of a token as an average of all preceding tokens in the context window: . # Toy example: B=4 batches, T=8 time steps, C=2 channels torch.manual_seed(1337) B, T, C = 4, 8, 2 x = torch.randn(B, T, C) xbow = torch.zeros((B, T, C)) for b in range(B): for t in range(T): xprev = x[b, : t + 1] # (t, C) xbow[b, t] = torch.mean(xprev, 0) . | Bottleneck: Explicit Python loops are extremely slow and do not scale. | . 4.2. Version 2: Matrix Multiplication Trick (Lower Triangular Weights) . Averaging can be expressed efficiently as matrix multiplication using a lower-triangular weight matrix: . wei = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)) wei = wei / wei.sum(1, keepdim=True) xbow2 = wei @ x # (T, T) @ (B, T, C) -> (B, T, C) . 4.3. Version 3: Adding Softmax (Data-Dependent Affinity) . Instead of uniform averaging weights, tokens should dynamically calculate how much “attention” they want to pay to past tokens based on their content: . torch.manual_seed(42) a = torch.tril(torch.ones(3, 3)) wei = torch.zeros(3, 3) wei = wei.masked_fill(a == 0, float("-inf")) wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1) . 4.4. Version 4: Scaled Self-Attention (Queries, Keys, Values) . Self-attention introduces three core linear projections for every token: . | Query ($Q$): What am I looking for? | Key ($K$): What do I contain? | Value ($V$): What information will I pass along if attended to? | . class Head(nn.Module): """One head of self-attention""" def __init__(self, head_size, n_embd, block_size): super().__init__() self.key = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False) self.query = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False) self.value = nn.Linear(n_embd, head_size, bias=False) self.register_buffer("tril", torch.tril(torch.ones(block_size, block_size))) self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.2) def forward(self, x): B, T, C = x.shape k = self.key(x) # (B, T, hs) q = self.query(x) # (B, T, hs) # Compute attention scores ("affinities") wei = ( q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) * (k.shape[-1] ** -0.5) ) # (B, T, hs) @ (B, hs, T) -> (B, T, T) wei = wei.masked_fill(self.tril[:T, :T] == 0, float("-inf")) # Causal mask wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1) wei = self.dropout(wei) # Perform the weighted aggregation of the values v = self.value(x) # (B, T, hs) out = wei @ v # (B, T, T) @ (B, T, hs) -> (B, T, hs) return out . | Why Scale? ($\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$): Dividing by the square root of the head size prevents variance from growing too large before Softmax, which would otherwise push gradients close to zero. | .

90.title: 5. Multi-Head Attention & The Complete Transformer Block
90.content: To let the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces simultaneously, multiple attention heads are concatenated: . class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module): """Multiple heads of self-attention in parallel""" def __init__(self, num_heads, head_size, n_embd, block_size): super().__init__() self.heads = nn.ModuleList( [Head(head_size, n_embd, block_size) for _ in range(num_heads)] ) self.proj = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd) self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.2) def forward(self, x): out = torch.cat([h(x) for h in self.heads], dim=-1) out = self.dropout(self.proj(out)) return out . 5.1. Feed-Forward Networks & Residual Connections . Each transformer block pairs attention with a position-wise Feed-Forward Network, wrapped in Residual Connections (skip connections) and Layer Normalization: . class Block(nn.Module): """Transformer block: communication followed by computation""" def __init__(self, n_embd, n_head, block_size): super().__init__() head_size = n_embd // n_head self.sa = MultiHeadAttention(n_head, head_size, n_embd, block_size) self.ffwd = FeedForward(n_embd) self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd) self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd) def forward(self, x): x = x + self.sa(self.ln1(x)) # Residual connection around attention x = x + self.ffwd(self.ln2(x)) # Residual connection around feed-forward return x .

91.title: 6. Summary of Key Architectural Takeaways
91.content: . | Autoregressive Masking: Ensures future tokens cannot communicate with past tokens during training. | Positional Embeddings: Combined with token embeddings (nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)) to give the model awareness of token order. | Scaling Law Foundation: Transitioning from character-level Bigram baselines to multi-head stacked transformer blocks mirrors the exact scaling architecture utilized in state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-2, GPT-3, and beyond). | .
