263.title: Recommender Systems: High-Level Guide
263.content: This document is an extensive technical guide to modern recommendation systems. It synthesizes the supplied materials on recommendation-system foundations, candidate generation, collaborative filtering, ranking, re-ranking, calibration, search, evaluation, moderation, graph neural networks, Transformers, cold start, bias, multi-armed bandits, multi-objective optimization, generative recommendation, and representative research papers. The central engineering problem is to select and order a small set of useful items from a very large catalog for a particular user, context, or query, while satisfying latency, quality, safety, diversity, business, and fairness constraints.

264.title: Contents
264.content: . | Recommendation-system foundations | Production funnel architecture | Data and feature representations | Candidate generation | Collaborative filtering and matrix factorization | Two-tower retrieval and approximate nearest neighbors | Ranking and learning to rank | Re-ranking and slate optimization | Calibration | Search and hybrid retrieval | Evaluation and loss functions | Bias, feedback loops, and fairness | Content moderation and integrity | Cold-start strategies | Popular neural architectures | Graph neural networks | Transformers and sequential recommendation | Multi-armed and contextual bandits | Multi-objective optimization | Generative recommendation and LLMs | Production challenges | Research-paper map | End-to-end reference architecture | Implementation blueprint | Final technical takeaways | .

265.title: Recommendation-system foundations
265.content: What is a recommendation system? . A recommendation system is a machine-learning system that estimates which items a user is likely to find useful, relevant, enjoyable, or valuable, and then presents a selected set of those items. An item may be: . | A movie, song, video, article, product, restaurant, job, advertisement, or social connection. | A search result or document. | A notification, explanation, image, or content collection. | A generated response or conversational suggestion. | . A recommendation request usually contains three conceptual components: . | Component | Meaning | Examples | . | User or query | The entity for which recommendations are generated | User ID, search query, device, location | . | Item or document | A candidate that may be recommended | Movie, product, video, restaurant | . | Representation | A numerical description used by models | Features, embeddings, graph vectors | . A system attempts to estimate a relevance or utility function: . \[\hat{r}(u, i, c) = f_\theta(u, i, c)\] where: . | $u$ is the user or user representation. | $i$ is the item. | $c$ is contextual information. | $f_\theta$ is a learned model. | $\hat{r}$ is a predicted relevance, engagement probability, utility, or score. | . Why recommendation systems are difficult . A production recommender must solve several problems simultaneously: . | The catalog may contain millions or billions of items. | Most user-item interactions are unobserved. | Feedback is often implicit rather than explicit. | Exposure is not random; users interact with what the system shows them. | Popular items receive more exposure and therefore more feedback. | New users and items have little or no history. | User preferences change over time. | Different objectives can conflict. | The system must often respond within a strict latency budget. | A recommendation can affect user behavior, creating feedback loops. | Safety, policy, legal, and fairness requirements may override engagement. | . Discovery, search, and recommendation . Search and recommendation are closely related but have different starting conditions. | Property | Search | Recommendation | . | Explicit intent | Usually provided by a query | Often inferred from behavior or context | . | User state | Query-centric | User-history and context-centric | . | Candidate set | Query-matching documents | Personalized catalog items | . | Main challenge | Interpret the query and retrieve relevant results | Infer preferences and balance relevance with discovery | . | Typical signals | Terms, semantic similarity, filters | History, embeddings, context, social graph, popularity | . Modern systems often combine both. Search activity can enrich a recommender, while recommendation models can personalize search results.

266.title: Production funnel architecture
266.content: The two-stage funnel . A common production architecture separates fast retrieval from expensive ranking: . OFFLINE SYSTEMS +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | Events and Data | Feature Pipelines | Model Training | +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | | v v v +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | Item Embeddings | User Features | Models and | ANN Indices | Feature Store | Checkpoints | +-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+ | v ONLINE REQUEST PATH +-------------------+ | User / Query | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Candidate | Generation | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ranking / Scoring | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Final List | +-------------------+ . The two stages have different optimization goals: . | Stage | Main goal | Typical model or method | . | Candidate generation | High recall at low latency | Matrix factorization, two-tower model, ANN, popularity retrieval | . | Ranking | High precision and utility | Logistic regression, GBDT, deep ranker, Transformer | . Candidate generation operates over a large catalog and must be efficient. Ranking receives a much smaller candidate set and can use richer features and more computationally expensive models. The four-stage funnel . Some production systems separate ranking into retrieval, filtering, scoring, and ordering: . +-------------------+ | Entire Catalog | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Retrieval | High Recall | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Filtering | Eligibility Rules | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Scoring | Personalized | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ordering | Diversity, Policy | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | User-Facing Slate | +-------------------+ . The four stages separate concerns: . | Retrieval finds a broad set of potentially relevant items. | Filtering removes items that cannot or should not be shown. | Scoring estimates relevance or expected utility. | Ordering constructs the final slate while considering diversity, novelty, freshness, policy, and business constraints. | . Multiple candidate generators . A production system often combines several candidate sources: . | Collaborative-filtering candidates. | Content-similarity candidates. | Trending and popular candidates. | Geographical candidates. | Social-graph candidates. | Search-derived candidates. | Recently viewed or continued items. | New-item exploration candidates. | Sponsored or business-priority candidates. | . These sources are merged into a common candidate pool. Their individual scores are not necessarily comparable, which is one reason a separate ranking model is used. Offline and online environments . The offline environment creates artifacts needed by online serving: . | Item and user embeddings. | ANN indices. | Feature-store values. | Trained model checkpoints. | Popularity statistics. | Calibration maps. | Policy and moderation classifiers. | Candidate-generator configurations. | . The online environment performs request-specific work: . | Resolve user and context. | Retrieve candidates. | Apply eligibility filters. | Fetch online features. | Score candidates. | Re-rank the slate. | Log exposure and outcomes. | .

267.title: Data and feature representations
267.content: Explicit and implicit feedback . Feedback can be explicit or implicit. | Feedback type | Examples | Strengths | Limitations | . | Explicit | Rating, like, dislike, save | Direct preference signal | Sparse and subject to rating behavior | . | Implicit | Click, view, purchase, dwell time | Abundant and naturally collected | Ambiguous; exposure affects observations | . | Negative feedback | Hide, skip, report, unsubscribe | Useful for filtering and preference modeling | Often sparse and not always comparable across users | . An impression without an interaction is not always a true negative. The user may not have noticed the item, may have lacked time, or may have preferred another visible item. Dense and sparse features . Dense features are continuous or numerical values: . | Age or normalized price. | Rating statistics. | Time since the last interaction. | Watch duration. | Device or network measurements. | . Sparse features are categorical identifiers or high-cardinality values: . | User ID. | Item ID. | Country. | Language. | Product category. | Artist ID. | Search terms. | . Sparse features are commonly mapped to trainable embeddings. Sparse ID | v Embedding Lookup Table | v Dense Vector | +--> Concatenate with numerical features | v Neural or ranking model . Univalent and multivalent features . A univalent feature has one value for an entity, such as a user’s primary language. A multivalent feature contains a set or sequence, such as genres associated with a movie or a user’s viewing history. A variable-length collection can be transformed into a fixed-width vector using pooling: . \[\mathbf{h}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_j\] where $\mathbf{e}_j$ is the embedding of the $j$-th element. Mean pooling is simple and scalable, but it discards order and may treat all events equally. More advanced systems use recency weighting, attention, RNNs, Transformers, or graph aggregation. Embeddings . An embedding is a learned numerical vector representing an entity or event. Embedding spaces can encode: . | Similarity between items. | Similarity between users. | User-item compatibility. | Semantic content. | Behavioral patterns. | Graph neighborhoods. | . Similarity may be measured using a dot product: . \[s(u, i) = \mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{i}\] or cosine similarity: . \[\text{cos}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{i}) = \frac{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{i}} {\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert_2\lVert\mathbf{i}\rVert_2}\] Embedding quality depends on the training objective, negative-sampling strategy, data coverage, and serving-time consistency. Feature stores and training-serving consistency . A feature store can provide a common definition of features for both training and serving. This reduces training-serving skew, where the model sees one representation during training and another during production inference. Important consistency requirements include: . | Identical transformations. | Identical normalization parameters. | Correct event-time semantics. | No future information leaking into historical examples. | Consistent missing-value handling. | Versioned feature definitions. | .

268.title: Candidate generation
268.content: Candidate generation reduces a large catalog to a manageable set of items that can be scored in later stages. Content-based filtering . Content-based filtering recommends items based on item characteristics and the user’s inferred profile. Examples of item features include: . | Text descriptions. | Genres. | Tags. | Images. | Audio features. | Actors, artists, or creators. | Product attributes. | . A content-based system can construct a user profile by aggregating features from items the user interacted with: . \[\mathbf{u} = \text{aggregate}(\{\mathbf{i}_j : j \in H_u\})\] where $H_u$ is the user’s interaction history. Advantages . | Can recommend new items when content features are available. | Does not require other users’ interactions. | Can personalize niche interests. | Is relatively easy to explain through item attributes. | . Limitations . | It may over-specialize in existing interests. | It requires useful item metadata. | It may lack serendipity. | It often requires domain-specific feature engineering. | . Collaborative filtering . Collaborative filtering uses interactions among users and items rather than item content alone. The central assumption is that users with similar behavior may prefer similar items, and items consumed by similar users may be related. User-item interactions | v +------------------------+ | Discover user patterns | and item patterns | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Learn latent vectors | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Retrieve or score | unseen items | +------------------------+ . Collaborative filtering can discover relationships that are not obvious from item metadata, but it is vulnerable to sparse data and cold start. Matrix factorization . A user-item interaction matrix can be approximated using latent user and item factors: . \[R \approx U V^{\top}\] The predicted interaction can be written as: . \[\hat{r}_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + \mathbf{p}_u^{\top}\mathbf{q}_i\] where: . | $\mu$ is the global bias. | $b_u$ and $b_i$ are user and item biases. | $\mathbf{p}_u$ is the user latent vector. | $\mathbf{q}_i$ is the item latent vector. | . The model may minimize squared error for explicit ratings or use a ranking loss for implicit feedback. Weighted alternating least squares . Weighted alternating least squares (WALS) is useful for large sparse interaction matrices. It alternates between solving for user factors while holding item factors fixed and solving for item factors while holding user factors fixed. A generic objective is: . \[\min_{U,V} \sum_{u,i} c_{ui}(p_{ui} - \mathbf{u}_u^{\top}\mathbf{v}_i)^2 + \lambda(\lVert U\rVert_F^2 + \lVert V\rVert_F^2)\] where $c_{ui}$ weights confidence in an observed or unobserved interaction. Negative sampling . Many recommender tasks have far more unobserved pairs than observed positive pairs. Negative sampling selects a manageable set of presumed negative examples. Common strategies include: . | Uniform random negatives. | Popularity-weighted negatives. | In-batch negatives. | Hard negatives from a retrieval model. | Time-aware negatives. | Exposure-aware negatives. | . Negative sampling changes the training distribution. Evaluation and serving should account for that difference.

269.title: Two-tower retrieval and approximate nearest neighbors
269.content: Two-tower architecture . A two-tower model independently encodes a user or query and an item: . +------------------+ +------------------+ | User features | Item features | +------------------+ +------------------+ | v v +------------------+ +------------------+ | User tower | Item tower | Neural encoder | Neural encoder | +------------------+ +------------------+ | v v +------------------+ +------------------+ | User embedding | Item embedding | +------------------+ +------------------+ \ / \ / v v Similarity function | v Retrieval score . The item tower can be run offline for the entire catalog. At request time, only the user tower and ANN lookup need to run. A typical loss encourages positive pairs to have high similarity and negatives to have lower similarity: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp(s(u, i^+)/\tau)} {\exp(s(u, i^+)/\tau) + \sum_{j \in N}\exp(s(u, i_j^-)/\tau)}\] where $\tau$ is a temperature parameter. Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval . Exact comparison of a query vector with every catalog vector is expensive. Approximate nearest-neighbor methods trade a small amount of recall for much lower latency. Common index families include: . | HNSW graphs. | Inverted-file indices. | Product quantization. | Tree-based indices. | Hybrid graph and quantization systems. | . Important ANN trade-offs include: . | Recall versus latency. | Memory versus compression. | Update speed versus query speed. | Index freshness versus rebuild cost. | . Candidate-generator evaluation . Candidate generation is usually evaluated using recall at a candidate-set size: . \[\text{Recall@K} = \frac{|\text{relevant items in top-}K|} {|\text{relevant items}|}\] High retrieval recall is necessary but not sufficient. A generator may retrieve relevant items but create a candidate set that is redundant, unsafe, stale, or difficult for later ranking to process.

270.title: Ranking and learning to rank
270.content: Scoring versus ranking . Scoring assigns an independent value to each candidate. Ranking orders candidates according to those scores or according to a list-level objective. A scoring model may estimate: . | Click probability. | Purchase probability. | Watch probability. | Expected watch time. | Conversion value. | Long-term satisfaction. | . A ranking model may then sort candidates, subject to additional constraints. Point-wise learning to rank . Point-wise methods treat each item independently as a regression or classification example. Examples include: . | Logistic regression. | Linear regression. | Gradient-boosted decision trees. | Neural networks. | . For binary engagement, binary cross-entropy is common: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} = -\left[y\log\hat{p} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{p})\right]\] Point-wise approaches are simple and scalable, but they do not directly model competition among items in the same slate. Pair-wise learning to rank . Pair-wise methods train on item pairs and attempt to place the preferred item above the less-preferred item. A pairwise logistic loss can be expressed as: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{pair}} = -\log \sigma(s(u, i^+) - s(u, i^-))\] Examples include RankNet, RankSVM, LambdaRank, and LambdaMART. Pair-wise approaches align more closely with ordering but may require many item pairs. List-wise learning to rank . List-wise methods optimize an entire candidate list or an approximation to a list-ranking metric. Examples include ListNet, ListMLE, SoftRank, and list-wise Lambda methods. They can better represent the final ranking objective but usually have higher computational and implementation complexity. Multi-stage ranking . Large platforms may use multiple ranking passes: . Candidate pool: 500 items | v First pass: lightweight model | v Top 150 items | v Second pass: richer model | v Top 50 items | v Final pass: deep model and constraints | v Top 25 items . The first pass prioritizes speed, while later passes use richer features and more expressive models. Objective-function design . The ranking objective determines what the system learns to optimize. Optimizing only one metric can create undesirable behavior: . | Objective | Possible failure mode | . | Click-through rate | Clickbait and shallow engagement | . | Watch time | Bias toward long content | . | Purchases | Reduced discovery or over-commercialization | . | Popularity | Feedback loops and reduced long-tail exposure | . | Short-term engagement | Lower long-term satisfaction | . Production rankers often combine several predicted outcomes and apply constraints or re-ranking after model scoring.

271.title: Re-ranking and slate optimization
271.content: Re-ranking operates after initial scoring and modifies the candidate order or removes candidates to satisfy additional goals. Common re-ranking objectives . | Diversity. | Freshness. | Novelty. | Serendipity. | Popularity control. | Seasonality. | Fairness. | Creator or seller coverage. | Safety and policy compliance. | Business constraints. | . Diversity . If the highest-scoring items are almost identical, the user may receive a repetitive slate. Diversity can be encouraged through: . | Category quotas. | Similarity penalties. | Maximum marginal relevance. | Multiple candidate generators. | Multiple rankers with different objectives. | Clustering and coverage constraints. | . A simple diversity-aware objective is: . \[\text{Utility}(S) = \sum_{i \in S} \text{relevance}(i) - \lambda \sum_{i,j \in S} \text{similarity}(i,j)\] where $S$ is the selected slate. Freshness and seasonality . Freshness can be modeled using a time-decay function: . \[w(t) = \exp(-\lambda \Delta t)\] where $\Delta t$ is the age of the item or event. Seasonality can be represented through: . | Day-of-week features. | Month or holiday indicators. | Historical performance during similar periods. | Time-aware models. | Event-specific rules. | . Popularity control . Popularity is useful for cold-start fallback and broad appeal, but excessive popularity weighting can suppress long-tail content. A re-ranker may normalize or penalize popularity so that relevant niche items receive exposure. Re-ranking as constrained selection . A practical formulation is: . \[\max_{S \subseteq C} U(S)\] subject to constraints such as: . | Size constraint: $|S| = K$. | At most $m$ items from one category. | At least one fresh item. | No policy-violating item. | Minimum creator or seller coverage. | .

272.title: Calibration
272.content: Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. If a model assigns a click probability of $0.7$ to a group of impressions, approximately 70% of that group should click for the model to be well calibrated. Calibration matters when probabilities are used for: . | Threshold decisions. | Risk-sensitive decisions. | Utility calculations. | Multi-objective combinations. | Budget allocation. | Downstream re-ranking. | . Platt scaling . Platt scaling fits a sigmoid mapping from a raw score $s$ to a probability: . \[P(y=1 \mid s) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(As+B)}\] The parameters $A$ and $B$ are learned on a held-out calibration set. Isotonic regression . Isotonic regression learns a non-decreasing mapping without assuming a sigmoid shape. It can be more flexible but may overfit when calibration data is limited. Bayesian calibration . Bayesian binning methods estimate event probabilities within score bins while incorporating uncertainty and priors. They can be useful when data is limited or estimates need uncertainty handling. Calibration evaluation . Common diagnostics include: . | Reliability diagrams. | Expected calibration error. | Maximum calibration error. | Brier score. | Log loss. | . Calibration should be evaluated by important slices, such as device, geography, language, user activity, item popularity, and traffic source.

273.title: Search and hybrid retrieval
273.content: Information retrieval . Information retrieval concerns representing, storing, organizing, and accessing information from large collections. A search system receives a query $q$ and a document collection $D$ and attempts to return a ranked subset of useful documents. Lexical search . Lexical search relies on term overlap. TF-IDF assigns a weight to a term based on its local frequency and global rarity: . \[\text{tfidf}(t,d) = \text{tf}(t,d) \cdot \log\left(\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}\right)\] BM25 improves term-based retrieval by incorporating term frequency saturation and document-length normalization. Strengths . | Fast lookup through inverted indices. | Strong performance for identifiers and exact terminology. | Good interpretability. | Mature ecosystem. | . Limitations . | Vocabulary mismatch. | Weak synonym and paraphrase handling. | Limited semantic understanding. | Difficulty with ambiguous intent. | . Semantic search . Semantic search encodes queries and documents into dense vectors and retrieves nearby vectors. It can handle: . | Synonyms. | Paraphrases. | Related concepts. | Cross-language or cross-modal relationships. | . Limitations include: . | Higher compute cost. | Larger storage requirements. | Harder explanations. | Potential overgeneralization. | Need for domain adaptation. | . Hybrid search . Hybrid search combines lexical and semantic retrieval: . User Query | +------------------+ | v v Lexical Retrieval Dense Retrieval | +--------+---------+ v Candidate Fusion | v Neural Reranking | v Final Results . Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines rankings without requiring directly comparable scores: . \[\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{1}{k + r_m(d)}\] where $r_m(d)$ is the rank of document $d$ in system $m$. Index structures . | Index | Mapping | Main use | . | Forward index | Document to terms | Reconstruction, metadata, snippets | . | Inverted index | Term to documents | Lexical retrieval | . | Embedding index | Vector to nearby vectors | Semantic retrieval | . Modern search systems may maintain all three.

274.title: Evaluation and loss functions
274.content: Offline evaluation . Offline evaluation typically involves: . | Define historical examples. | Split data by time or user appropriately. | Train candidate models. | Evaluate on held-out interactions. | Compare metrics and slices. | Check leakage and bias. | Select candidates for online testing. | . Random splitting can produce overly optimistic results when future interactions leak into training or when users appear in both sets in unrealistic ways. Online evaluation . Online evaluation uses live traffic, typically through: . | A/B tests. | Interleaving. | Contextual bandits. | Holdout groups. | Gradual rollouts. | . Online metrics should include guardrails, not only the primary objective. Precision and recall . \[\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\] \[\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\] At a cutoff $K$: . \[\text{Precision@K} = \frac{\text{relevant items in top }K}{K}\] \[\text{Recall@K} = \frac{\text{relevant items in top }K}{\text{total relevant items}}\] Mean reciprocal rank . MRR emphasizes the position of the first relevant item: . \[\text{MRR} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1}{\text{rank}_j}\] It ignores later relevant items after the first one. Average precision and mean average precision . Average precision rewards relevant items appearing early and averages precision at relevant positions. Mean average precision averages AP across queries or users. NDCG . Discounted cumulative gain discounts lower-ranked items: . \[\text{DCG@K} = \sum_{r=1}^{K}\frac{2^{rel_r}-1}{\log_2(r+1)}\] NDCG normalizes DCG by the ideal DCG: . \[\text{NDCG@K} = \frac{\text{DCG@K}}{\text{IDCG@K}}\] NDCG is useful when relevance is graded and rank position matters. Business and engagement metrics . Possible metrics include: . | Click-through rate. | Conversion rate. | Session length. | Dwell time. | Completion rate. | Repeat visits. | Retention. | Revenue or margin. | Creator coverage. | Catalog coverage. | Diversity. | Complaint or report rate. | Unsubscribe or disable rate. | . No single metric captures recommendation quality. A metric should be selected according to the product objective and evaluated with guardrails. Common loss functions . | Task | Typical loss | . | Binary engagement | Binary cross-entropy | . | Rating prediction | Mean squared error or mean absolute error | . | Pairwise preference | Pairwise logistic or hinge loss | . | Representation learning | Contrastive or triplet loss | . | List ranking | List-wise ranking loss | . | Diversity | Diversity regularizer or slate objective | . | Fairness | Group or exposure constraint loss | .

275.title: Bias, feedback loops, and fairness
275.content: Position bias . Items shown higher in a list often receive more attention regardless of intrinsic relevance. This creates a confound between position and relevance. Possible mitigations include: . | Randomized exposure experiments. | Inverse propensity weighting. | Position-aware click models. | Interleaving. | Position features used carefully during training. | Counterfactual evaluation. | . Inverse propensity weighting uses: . \[w_i = \frac{1}{P(\text{exposure}_i)}\] Care is required because low-propensity examples receive high weights and can increase variance. Popularity bias . Popularity bias causes popular items to receive more exposure, interactions, and future recommendations. This can suppress niche content and create a self-reinforcing loop. Possible mitigations include: . | Popularity-aware sampling. | Logit adjustment. | Long-tail exploration. | Exposure constraints. | Diversity-aware re-ranking. | Separate evaluation by popularity bucket. | . Selection bias . The training data contains interactions only for items that were exposed. Unexposed items provide little or no direct feedback, so the model may mistake lack of interaction for lack of relevance. Selection bias can be studied through: . | Exposure logs. | Propensity estimation. | Randomized traffic. | IPS or doubly robust estimators. | Counterfactual evaluation. | . Duration bias . If watch time is optimized directly, longer videos may appear better simply because they have more time available to accumulate watch time. Possible mitigations include: . | Completion rate. | Relative watch-time quantiles within duration buckets. | Normalized watch time. | Multi-objective objectives. | Separate short-form and long-form modeling. | . Clickbait bias . Click optimization can reward sensational content that attracts clicks but produces poor satisfaction. Weighted objectives can incorporate watch quality, completion, reports, or long-term engagement. Single-interest bias . A system may overrepresent a user’s most frequent interest and neglect other interests. Mitigations include: . | Interest-aware user representations. | Diversity constraints. | Multiple interest vectors. | Calibrated probability distributions. | Exploration policies. | Topic or category coverage metrics. | . Fairness . Fairness can concern: . | Equal opportunity for creators or sellers. | Exposure across item groups. | User-group performance parity. | Content safety and accessibility. | Geographic or language coverage. | . Fairness should be evaluated alongside utility, because improving one dimension can affect another.

276.title: Content moderation and integrity
276.content: Engagement alone is not an acceptable recommendation objective when content can cause harm. A moderation-aware funnel can be structured as follows: . +-------------------+ | Content Ingestion | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Input Moderation | Classifiers | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Eligible Catalog | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Retrieval | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Ranking | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Final Safety | and Policy Checks | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | User Presentation | +-------------------+ . Moderation may include: . | Automated classifiers. | Human review. | User reporting. | Appeals. | Age and region policies. | Copyright enforcement. | Hate-speech detection. | Child-safety protections. | Misinformation policies. | Spam and coordinated inauthentic behavior detection. | . Moderation can occur at multiple points: . | At content ingestion. | Before candidate retrieval. | After retrieval. | During ranking or re-ranking. | Immediately before presentation. | After user reports or post-publication review. | . A content item can be removed, down-ranked, age-gated, region-restricted, or routed for human review depending on policy.

277.title: Cold-start strategies
277.content: Cold start occurs when the system lacks enough interaction data to personalize effectively. Item cold start . New items can be represented using content features: . | Text embeddings. | Image or audio embeddings. | Metadata. | Category information. | Creator or seller attributes. | Knowledge-based rules. | . This makes content-based and hybrid systems useful for newly added items. User cold start . New users can be handled using: . | Popular items. | Geography or language-specific popularity. | Demographic or contextual priors. | Onboarding surveys. | Preference elicitation. | Active learning. | Session-level behavior. | Search queries. | . A practical transition is: . New User | v Popular and Contextual Candidates | v Onboarding or Early Interactions | v Session Representation | v Personalized Retrieval and Ranking . Community or marketplace cold start . A new marketplace has both new users and new items. Possible strategies include: . | Early-adopter programs. | Internal testing. | Employee dogfooding. | Beta releases. | Transfer from similar markets. | Rules and domain knowledge. | Targeted exploration. | . Feature hashing . Feature hashing maps high-cardinality identifiers into a fixed number of buckets. It reduces memory but introduces possible collisions. A signed hashing scheme or multiple hash functions can reduce systematic collision effects. Hashing is useful for managing dynamic categories, but collision analysis and monitoring are important.

278.title: Popular neural architectures
278.content: Wide and Deep . Wide and Deep combines: . | A wide component for memorization of explicit feature crosses. | A deep component for generalization through embeddings and nonlinear layers. | . Sparse Features | +----------------------+ | v v +--------------+ +--------------+ | Wide Model | Deep Model | Crosses | Embeddings | +--------------+ +--------------+ | +----------+-----------+ v Combined Prediction . The wide side can memorize specific interactions such as user-category combinations. The deep side can generalize to related but unseen combinations. Factorization machines . Factorization Machines model pairwise feature interactions using latent vectors: . \[\hat{y} = w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j\rangle x_i x_j\] They are effective for sparse, high-dimensional features and can incorporate user, item, and context variables. DeepFM . DeepFM combines a factorization-machine component with a deep neural network. The FM part captures pairwise interactions, while the deep part models higher-order nonlinear relationships. Neural Collaborative Filtering . NCF replaces the simple matrix-factorization inner product with a neural interaction function. User and item embeddings are combined and passed through an MLP. Deep and Cross Networks . DCN learns explicit feature crosses through a cross network rather than requiring manual cross-feature engineering. The deep component provides generalization. DLRM . Deep Learning Recommendation Models typically use embedding tables for sparse features, dense feature processing, feature interaction, and an MLP prediction tower. They are common in large-scale click and conversion prediction. When deep learning may not help . Deep models are not always better. Simpler models may win when: . | Data is sparse. | The dataset is small. | Features are homogeneous. | Latency constraints are strict. | Interpretability is essential. | A well-tuned linear or tree model already captures the available signal. | .

279.title: Graph neural networks
279.content: Graph representation . A recommendation graph may contain: . | User nodes. | Item nodes. | Creator or seller nodes. | Category nodes. | Query nodes. | Interaction edges. | Purchase, click, follow, or friendship edges. | . A user-item system is often represented as a bipartite graph. User A -------- Item 1 | | +---------- Item 2 User B -------- Item 2 | +---------- Item 3 . Message passing . A generic graph-convolution layer aggregates neighbor information: . \[\mathbf{h}_v^{(l+1)} = \phi\left( W_0^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_v^{(l)} + \text{AGG}_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)} W_1^{(l)}\mathbf{h}_u^{(l)} \right)\] where $\mathcal{N}(v)$ is the neighborhood of node $v$. The process consists of: . | Compute messages. | Aggregate messages. | Transform the aggregate. | Update the node representation. | Repeat across layers. | . GCNs, GATs, and GraphSAGE . | Architecture | Main idea | RecSys value | . | GCN | Aggregate neighborhood features | Captures relational structure | . | GAT | Learn attention weights over neighbors | Focuses on important relationships | . | GraphSAGE | Sample and aggregate neighbors | Supports scalable and inductive learning | . | Edge-aware GNN | Uses edge attributes in message passing | Models interaction type and strength | . GraphSAGE is particularly useful for new nodes because it can generate representations from features and sampled neighborhoods rather than requiring a learned vector for every node. Graph losses . Possible objectives include: . | Node classification loss. | Link-prediction binary cross-entropy. | Pairwise ranking loss. | Triplet loss. | Graph reconstruction loss. | Regularization losses. | . For a positive user-item edge and a negative sampled edge: . \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{margin}} = \max\left(0, m - s(u,i^+) + s(u,i^-) \right)\] where $m$ is a margin. Graph recommender workflow . User-item events | v Construct graph | v Sample neighborhoods | v Run message passing | v Generate user/item embeddings | v Score unseen edges | v Retrieve and rank items . Industry patterns . Graph-based recommendation is useful for: . | Social friend and story ranking. | Item discovery. | Food and restaurant recommendations. | Related content. | Pinterest-style visual discovery. | Search and entity relationships. | . Graph models can improve relational understanding, but they also introduce costs related to graph storage, neighborhood sampling, freshness, and distributed training.

280.title: Transformers and sequential recommendation
280.content: Why sequences matter . A user’s recent actions may reveal short-term intent that differs from long-term preferences. Order, timing, and the relationship between events can therefore matter. Pooling treats events as an unordered collection. Sequential models can represent: . | Recency. | Repeated patterns. | Session intent. | Transition probabilities. | Long-range dependencies. | . Transformer self-attention . For queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$, scaled dot-product attention is: . \[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\] Self-attention allows an event to use information from other events in the sequence. Sequential recommendation pipeline . Ordered interaction history | v +--------------------------+ | Item and event embeddings| +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Positional or temporal | information | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Transformer encoder | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | User or session vector | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | Candidate scoring | +--------------------------+ . RNNs and GRUs . RNNs and GRUs process event sequences recurrently. They can be effective for short sessions but have sequential computation and may struggle with long histories. Behavioral Sequence Transformer . A ranking model can condition on a user’s behavior sequence and a target item, predicting the probability of engagement. The target item can be marked or included alongside the historical sequence. Multimodal and multitask Transformers . Modern systems may combine: . | Text embeddings. | Image embeddings. | Audio embeddings. | Product or item metadata. | User history. | Search queries. | Multiple engagement labels. | . Multitask training can improve sparse objectives by sharing representations across clicks, saves, purchases, and other events.

281.title: Multi-armed and contextual bandits
281.content: Multi-armed bandit problem . A bandit chooses an action from a set of arms and observes a reward. The objective is to maximize cumulative reward while balancing exploration and exploitation. \[\max \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t\right]\] Regret compares the reward obtained with the reward that would have been obtained by always choosing the best action. Epsilon-greedy . With probability $\epsilon$, choose an exploratory action. With probability $1-\epsilon$, choose the action with the highest estimated reward. Upper confidence bound . UCB selects an action using both estimated reward and uncertainty: . \[\text{UCB}_i(t) = \hat{\mu}_i(t) + c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{n_i(t)} }\] where $n_i(t)$ is the number of times arm $i$ has been selected. Thompson sampling . Thompson sampling maintains a posterior distribution over each arm’s reward and samples from those posteriors to select actions. Contextual bandits . Contextual bandits condition the action choice on user and environment context: . \[a_t = \pi(x_t)\] where $x_t$ may include: . | User attributes. | Device. | Time. | Location. | Recent history. | Item context. | . Contextual bandits are useful when different users respond differently to the same candidate. Bandits in recommendation systems . Bandits can be used for: . | Exploration of long-tail items. | Personalization. | Testing variants. | Recommendation explanations. | Artwork selection. | Cuisine discovery. | Dynamic content selection. | Cold-start items. | . Off-policy evaluation . Historical logs are generated by an old policy, but the goal is to estimate a new policy. Inverse propensity scoring can estimate counterfactual reward when exposure probabilities are known or estimated: . \[\hat{V}_{\text{IPS}}(\pi) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{\mathbb{1}[a_t = \pi(x_t)]r_t} {p(a_t\mid x_t)}\] High variance is a major challenge. Self-normalized and doubly robust estimators can reduce some problems. Bandits versus A/B testing . | Property | A/B testing | Bandit testing | . | Allocation | Usually fixed | Adapts over time | . | Interpretation | Straightforward | More complex | . | Exploration | Controlled by experiment design | Built into policy | . | Underperforming variants | Continue receiving assigned traffic | Can receive less traffic | . | Best use | Clear statistical comparison | Continuous adaptation and personalization | .

282.title: Multi-objective optimization
282.content: A recommender may need to optimize several objectives: . | Relevance. | Engagement. | Diversity. | Freshness. | Creator coverage. | Revenue. | Long-term retention. | Safety. | Fairness. | . These objectives can conflict. Multi-objective optimization seeks Pareto-optimal trade-offs: improving one objective further would worsen at least one other objective. A weighted model may be written as: . \[S(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j s_j(i)\] where $s_j$ are objective-specific scores and $w_j$ are tunable weights. Constrained optimization . A primary metric can be optimized subject to guardrails: . \[\max_x m_1(x)\] subject to: . \[m_j(x) \ge c_j, \quad j=2,\dots,m\] or, for safety constraints: . \[\text{violation}(x) \le \epsilon\] MOO versus MAB . | Concept | Multi-objective optimization | Multi-armed bandit | . | Core problem | Balance conflicting objectives | Explore and exploit uncertain actions | . | Typical setting | Static or periodically tuned | Sequential and adaptive | . | Output | Pareto set or weighted policy | Action-selection policy | . | Example | Relevance versus diversity | Explore new items versus exploit known items | .

283.title: Generative recommendation and LLMs
283.content: The generative shift . Traditional recommenders score or rank known items. Generative recommenders model recommendation as conditional generation: . \[\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y} p(y \mid C)\] where $C$ includes user history, context, item metadata, queries, or retrieved information. The generated output may be: . | An item identifier. | A sequence of item identifiers. | A semantic item ID. | A natural-language explanation. | A conversational recommendation. | A multimodal recommendation artifact. | . Semantic IDs . Semantic IDs represent items as sequences of discrete codes derived from content embeddings, often through residual vector quantization. Item content | v Dense item embedding | v Residual quantization | v Semantic ID tokens | v Autoregressive recommendation model . A Semantic ID can be represented as: . \[\text{SID}(i) = (c_1,c_2,\dots,c_L)\] where each $c_l$ is selected from a learned codebook. Semantic IDs may improve generalization to new or long-tail items because related items can share code structure. Hybrid dense-generative systems . A practical architecture may combine dense retrieval with an LLM or generative ranker: . User context | +----------------------+ | v v Dense retrieval Context and metadata | +----------+-----------+ v Candidate set | v Generative ranker | v Explanation and slate . Retrieval provides grounding and scalability. Generative models provide contextual reasoning, explanation, and flexible interaction. Retrieval-augmented recommendation . A retrieval-augmented recommender retrieves relevant catalog, profile, or policy context before generating a recommendation or explanation. This can reduce hallucination and improve factual grounding, but it introduces: . | Additional latency. | Retrieval-quality dependence. | Context-window constraints. | Privacy and authorization requirements. | More complex evaluation. | . LLM use cases in recommendation . LLMs may support: . | Query understanding. | Catalog enrichment. | Item summarization. | Natural-language explanations. | Conversational preference elicitation. | Cold-start item representation. | Cross-domain transfer. | Semantic ID generation. | Agentic recommendation workflows. | . LLMs should not replace all specialized models automatically. A production design must consider latency, cost, controllability, privacy, and the need for exact catalog grounding.

284.title: Production challenges
284.content: Offline-online mismatch . A model can improve offline metrics but perform worse online because of: . | Distribution shift. | Exposure bias. | Metric misalignment. | Training-serving skew. | Feedback loops. | User adaptation. | Latency or timeout behavior. | Differences in candidate availability. | . Reproducibility . Reproducible training requires versioning: . | Code. | Data. | Features. | Dependencies. | Random seeds. | Model configurations. | Training environment. | Evaluation scripts. | . Model freshness . User preferences and item popularity change. Systems may use: . | Periodic retraining. | Incremental updates. | Online learning. | Streaming features. | Time-decay features. | Bandit exploration. | . Latency . Latency can be improved through: . | Smaller first-stage models. | ANN retrieval. | Caching. | Batching. | Parallel candidate generators. | Quantization. | Distillation. | Feature precomputation. | Asynchronous enrichment. | Efficient serving infrastructure. | . Feature and model failures . A new feature can reduce performance if it introduces noise, leakage, or a mismatch with the target objective. Feature changes should be tested offline and online, with slice analysis and rollback capability. Monitoring . 290.title: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking: Modern Architectures for Relevant AI Systems (in late 2026)
290.content: Primary references: . | Bypassing inference bottlenecks: Accelerating complex AI search with Retrieve-for-Train | Make Retrieval / Search More Relevant With An LLM | GenRec: Towards LLM-Native Recommendation at Netflix | . Modern search and recommendation systems are moving beyond a single embedding similarity score. Production systems increasingly combine structured query understanding, hard metadata filtering, semantic retrieval, learned ranking, catalog constraints, and personalization. This document covers three complementary patterns: . | Retrieve-for-Train: compile expensive retrieval reasoning into a lightweight, single-pass retriever. | Search-expert: convert natural-language queries into structured filters before semantic retrieval. | GenRec: use an LLM-backed ranker with catalog-aware scoring for large-scale recommendation. | . A note on source coverage: the ACM paper, several arXiv papers, LinkedIn engineering posts, Pinterest and Instacart posts, Spotify research, and Perplexity Photon links provided could not be fully verified from their primary pages in this pass. This document therefore focuses in depth on the three accessible primary sources above and treats the remaining links as a reading list rather than as verified technical claims.

291.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
291.title: Part 1: Foundations

292.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
292.title: Search versus recommendation
292.content: Search and recommendation solve related but different problems. | Dimension | Search | Recommendation | . | Primary input | Explicit user query | User history, context, and candidate inventory | . | Primary goal | Satisfy the stated intent | Maximize long-term user value | . | Typical output | Ranked results for a query | Personalized ranked slate | . | Hard constraints | Often explicit: price, color, availability | Often business or policy constraints | . | Main challenge | Interpreting intent correctly | Balancing relevance, diversity, and long-term satisfaction | . | Feedback signal | Clicks, conversions, reformulations | Plays, watch time, saves, skips, retention | . A search query such as “noise cancelling headphones any colour but black, under $300, with a 4 star rating” contains both semantic intent and hard constraints. A recommendation request may contain no explicit query at all, but must still respect catalog, business, and personalization constraints. sarthakai.substack .

293.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
293.title: The modern retrieval stack
293.content: A common production pattern is: . Natural-language query | v +---------------------------+ | Query understanding | - intent | - entities | - filters | - language | - reformulation | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Structured pre-filtering | - price | - color | - availability | - category | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Semantic retrieval | - vector search | - lexical search | - hybrid retrieval | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Ranking / reranking | - relevance | - personalization | - business constraints | - diversity | +-------------+-------------+ | v Ranked results . This pipeline separates concerns: . | Query understanding decides what the user means. | Filtering enforces non-negotiable constraints. | Retrieval finds semantically relevant candidates. | Ranking orders candidates using relevance, personalization, and business objectives. | . Search-expert frames this as structured pre-filtering followed by approximate nearest-neighbor vector search and a learning-to-rank reranker. sarthakai.substack .

294.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
294.title: Part 2: Query Understanding as Structured Extraction

295.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
295.title: The problem
295.content: Natural-language queries often contain implicit filters that a semantic retriever may treat as soft preferences rather than hard rules. For example: . noise cancelling headphones any colour but black, under $200 and over 4 stars . A pure vector-search system may return semantically similar headphones that are black, cost more than $200, or have a rating below 4 stars. The embeddings capture meaning, but they do not naturally enforce constraints. Search-expert addresses this by converting the query into structured fields before retrieval: . { "product": "headphones", "feature": "noise cancelling", "color": ["ne:black"], "price": "lt:200", "rating": "gte:4" } . The structured output uses explicit operators such as lt:, gte:, ne:, and between:100:200, so downstream systems can translate it into filters for Elasticsearch, SQL, ChromaDB, Pinecone, or another backend. sarthakai.substack .

296.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
296.title: Why structured extraction matters
296.content: Structured extraction enables a hybrid retrieval pipeline: . Natural-language query | v Structured extraction | v Hard metadata filters | v Vector search within filtered candidates | v Semantic ranking | v Ranked results . The hard filters ensure that a $400 product is not returned when the user asked for “under $200.” Vector search then ranks the surviving candidates by semantic relevance. sarthakai.substack .

297.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
297.title: Search-expert design
297.content: Search-expert is an 800M-parameter small language model, search-expert-json-0.8b, fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-0.8B using LoRA. It converts a natural-language search query into structured JSON. sarthakai.substack . | Property | Value | . | Base model | Qwen3.5-0.8B | . | Model size | 800M parameters | . | Fine-tuning method | LoRA | . | LoRA rank | 16 | . | LoRA alpha | 16 | . | Trainable parameters | 0.74% | . | Quantization | 4-bit NF4 | . | Approximate VRAM footprint | 1–2 GB | . | Training framework | Unsloth FastLanguageModel | . | Training data | 100,000 synthetic query-structured-output pairs | . | Domains | E-commerce, real estate, flights, hotels, jobs, cars, restaurants, movies, healthcare, courses | . | Reported key F1 | 0.913 | . | Reported parse rate | 98.2% | . The model is trained to output only fields explicitly present in the query, reducing hallucinated fields. A separate LoRA adapter is trained for each serialization format, such as JSON or YAML. sarthakai.substack .

298.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
298.title: Training configuration
298.content: The published training setup uses: sarthakai.substack . Effective batch size: 16 Per-device batch size: 8 Gradient accumulation: 2 Training steps: 300 Learning-rate schedule: Cosine Warmup steps: 100 Peak learning rate: 2e-4 Optimizer: AdamW 8-bit Maximum sequence length: 512 tokens Sequence packing: Enabled . LoRA adapters are injected into: . q_proj k_proj v_proj o_proj gate_proj up_proj down_proj . This is a practical demonstration that a small, domain-specialized model can perform constrained structured extraction reliably. The author explicitly argues that the task is bounded enough that a purpose-trained small model can outperform a general-purpose large model in cost, speed, and consistency. sarthakai.substack .

299.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
299.title: Constraint-satisfaction benchmark
299.content: Search-expert was evaluated on 25 complex, multi-constraint Amazon search queries. The evaluation measured whether the top six results satisfied the user’s hard constraints. sarthakai.substack . | Pipeline | Overall constraint satisfaction | Perfect@6 | . | Hybrid: search-expert plus filtered vector search | 1.00 | 1.00 | . | Amazon search | 0.76 | 0.42 | . | Pure vector search | 0.56 | 0.21 | . The hybrid pipeline achieved perfect price satisfaction, color exclusion, and color match across the evaluated queries. Pure vector search performed worst because embedding similarity treats constraints such as color and price as soft semantic signals rather than enforceable rules. sarthakai.substack . These results are specific to the author’s benchmark, query set, product pool, and retrieval configuration. They should not be generalized as universal superiority over any production search engine.

300.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
300.title: Text-to-SQL versus semantic search
300.content: Search-expert draws an important distinction: . | Approach | Strength | Limitation | . | Text-to-SQL | Exact lookup over structured data | Does not rank by semantic relevance | . | Pure vector search | Understands unstructured meaning | Treats hard constraints as soft signals | . | Hybrid retrieval | Enforces constraints, then ranks semantically | Requires query understanding and more infrastructure | . The production pattern is therefore: . structured extraction → hard metadata filters → vector search within filtered set → semantic ranking . Search is not merely “which rows match?” It is “which items are most relevant?” Relevance includes both structured constraints and unstructured meaning. sarthakai.substack .

301.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
301.title: Part 3: Retrieve-for-Train

302.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
302.title: The inference bottleneck
302.content: Complex AI search often requires query fan-out: breaking one broad prompt into several related sub-queries to retrieve a coherent set of results. For example, a query such as “camping gear” should not return ten slight variations of four-person tents. It should return a complementary slate: a tent, sleeping bag, portable stove, and headlamp. research . Google Research identifies two problems with using a general LLM for this at inference time: . | Paraphrastic collapse: the model generates near-synonymous queries instead of complementary facets. | Autoregressive latency: the model spends a large thinking budget generating intermediate reasoning tokens before producing search terms. research | . For example, given “Bohemian festival style,” a zero-shot LLM may generate: . - bohemian festival fashion - bohemian festival clothes . These are redundant paraphrases. A more useful fan-out might include distinct facets such as: . - fringe jackets - crochet dresses - suede boots . The second set covers complementary dimensions of the original intent. research .

303.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
303.title: Retrieve-for-Train idea
303.content: Retrieve-for-Train moves the expensive exploration offline. Instead of forcing an LLM to reason at inference time, it uses offline reinforcement learning once to learn reward-aligned query fan-outs, then distills that behavior into a lightweight retriever. research . Broad query | v +---------------------------+ | Fan-out language model | Trained once with RL | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Supervision synthesis | query -> target-set pairs | +-------------+-------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Diffusion retriever | Single-pass fan-out | +-------------+-------------+ | v Set of target embeddings . This is a conceptual reconstruction of the three-step framework described by Google Research. research .

304.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
304.title: Three-stage pipeline
304.content: | Stage | Purpose | Output | . | Fan-out language model training | Learn property-aligned sub-queries with reinforcement learning | Fan-out language model | . | Supervision synthesis | Generate query-to-target-set pairs offline | Supervision data | . | Diffusive retriever training | Learn to map query embeddings to target embeddings | Lightweight diffusion retriever | . The fan-out language models used were 4B open-source models: Gemma3-4B and Qwen3-4B. Each generated exactly 10 sub-queries for every main search prompt. research . The final diffusion retriever has 53.9M parameters and maps a query embedding directly to a complete set of target embeddings in one non-autoregressive pass. research .

305.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
305.title: Set-level rewards
305.content: Traditional learning-to-rank evaluates items independently. Retrieve-for-Train optimizes properties that exist only at the set level. The composite reward balances: research . | Property | Meaning | Failure it prevents | . | Groundedness | Generated sub-queries correspond to retrievable database items | Nonsense strings that exploit embedding coordinates | . | Diversity | The sub-query set covers broad semantic breadth | Repetitive paraphrases | . | Alignment | Sub-queries remain related to the original prompt | Semantic drift | . Diversity is measured using the Vendi Score over the entire set of sub-queries. research . These rewards act as mutual counter-anchors: . | Groundedness alone can reward degenerate strings. | Alignment alone can reward repetitive paraphrases. | Diversity forces the model to explore distinct, useful directions. research | .

306.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
306.title: Training method
306.content: Google Research uses Soft-GRPO, combining group relative policy optimization with soft proximal policy optimization regularization. The fan-out language model is optimized against the composite reward. research . The important architectural insight is that reinforcement learning is used as a one-time objective transducer, not as an online inference engine. The expensive reward-driven exploration happens during training; the deployed retriever performs a fast single-pass mapping. research .

307.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
307.title: Results
307.content: Retrieve-for-Train was evaluated on: . | Open-ended abstract retrieval, where quality is measured by set-level properties such as diversity, alignment, and groundedness. | Weakly supervised compositional retrieval, where queries are paired with a weak reference set. research | . The evaluation used: . | A fashion dataset of user-curated outfits, evaluated with a CLIP-based retriever. | A proprietary industrial dataset of expert-generated music playlists, evaluated with MuLan. research | . Reported results: . | Outcome | Retrieve-for-Train result | . | Retrieval quality | Outperformed single-query search, zero-shot expansion, and Best-of-N baselines | . | Inference speed | 12 to 20 times faster than autoregressive approaches | . | Large-batch latency | Autoregressive fan-out approached 50 seconds; diffusion remained sub-second to a few seconds | . | Model size | Final diffusion retriever: 53.9M parameters | . | Fan-out models | Gemma3-4B and Qwen3-4B | . | Sub-queries per prompt | 10 | . These results are from Google Research’s described experiments and should be interpreted in the context of their datasets, embedding backbones, and retrieval tasks. research .

308.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
308.title: Why this matters
308.content: Retrieve-for-Train shows that expensive reasoning does not need to happen at inference time. A system can use a large model and reinforcement learning offline to discover good behavior, then compile that behavior into a much smaller, faster model. This is analogous to using a teacher model offline and deploying a student model online: . Large reasoner + reward model | offline training v Compact retriever | online inference v Fast, property-aligned retrieval .

309.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
309.title: Part 4: GenRec and LLM-Native Recommendation

310.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
310.title: The recommendation problem
310.content: Netflix’s GenRec addresses full-catalog ranking: given a user $u$, interaction history $H$, current context $\tau$, and time $t$, produce a ranking $\pi$ over catalog items $C$. netflixtechblog . Formally: . \[(u, \tau, t, H) \rightarrow \pi\] where $\pi(i)$ is the position assigned to item $i$. The objective is expected long-term member utility, not merely short-term engagement. netflixtechblog .

311.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
311.title: Why traditional recommenders become complex
311.content: Netflix describes its prior production stack as relying on thousands of hand-crafted features over users, items, and interactions, plus specialized architectures for sequence modeling, feature interactions, and multi-task objectives. Adding a new content type or surface can require substantial feature engineering, architecture change, infrastructure work, and experimentation. netflixtechblog . LLMs offer a different approach: represent user histories and item metadata as text, capture relationships in a shared semantic space, and steer behavior through natural-language prompts. netflixtechblog . However, off-the-shelf LLMs are not production recommenders. Netflix identifies four issues: . | Over-recommending globally popular content. | Hallucinating out-of-catalog items. | Ignoring business constraints. | Providing limited personalization. netflixtechblog | .

312.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
312.title: GenRec architecture
312.content: GenRec is an LLM-backed recommendation ranker. It post-trains an internal foundation LLM on Netflix-specific data and objectives, then adds a catalog-aware scoring head. netflixtechblog . User history + context + item metadata | v [ Verbalized context ] | v [ Foundation LLM backbone ] | v [ Catalog-aware scoring head ] | v In-catalog item scores | v Personalized ranking . At inference time, GenRec feeds verbalized context into the model and applies the catalog-aware scoring head. It does not decode assistant messages. The conversational format is primarily a training-time device to preserve language understanding. netflixtechblog .

313.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
313.title: Two-phase training
313.content: GenRec uses a two-phase framework. netflixtechblog . | Phase | Purpose | Update frequency | . | Phase 1 | Adapt an open-source LLM on proprietary corpora to create a domain-aware backbone | Relatively infrequent | . | Phase 2 | Post-train the backbone on ranking-specific data and objectives | More frequent | . Netflix members generate hundreds of billions of interaction events across surfaces, including views, plays, durations, thumbs up or down, add-to-list actions, and abandons. These logs are converted into single-turn or multi-turn conversations between a user and a recommender. netflixtechblog .

314.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
314.title: Context engineering
314.content: Naively verbalizing every interaction would exceed the token budget. Netflix treats the context window as a new feature budget and applies context engineering. netflixtechblog . The approach is: . | Prioritize recent, high-signal history. | Compress or drop older history. | Structure prompts to maximize shared prefixes. | Enable better prefix caching. | Preserve ranking quality while reducing serving cost. netflixtechblog | . In experiments, Netflix reduced context tokens to roughly one-third of the original budget with negligible degradation in offline ranking metrics. Because serving cost is approximately proportional to context length, serving cost fell similarly. netflixtechblog .

315.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
315.title: Training objectives
315.content: GenRec uses a multi-objective loss combining: netflixtechblog . | A recommendation ranking objective. | Language-modeling objectives. | Alignment through reward-weighted training. | . The ranking objective uses cross-entropy over the catalog or candidate set. Positives are derived from high-value engagements, such as sufficiently long plays or strong explicit feedback, with thresholds and denoising logic. netflixtechblog . The language-modeling objective preserves general language understanding and keeps open the possibility of text-generation use cases such as recommendation explanations. netflixtechblog .

316.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
316.title: Reward-weighted alignment
316.content: Training only on raw interaction sequences can cause undesirable behavior, such as over-favoring binge-watching or over-focusing on one content type. GenRec weights the ranking loss using signals from separate reward models. netflixtechblog . \[\mathcal{L}_{weighted} = w_i \cdot \mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}\] where: . | $w_i$ is a scalar reward-derived weight for example $i$. | $\mathcal{L}_{ranking}^{(i)}$ is the ranking loss for that example. | . High-value engagements receive larger weights; low-value engagements are down-weighted. Netflix describes this as simpler and more cost-efficient than full reinforcement learning, while noting that RL-style methods such as GRPO produced additional gains but were deferred due to cost. netflixtechblog .

317.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
317.title: Catalog-aware scoring
317.content: GenRec’s architecture follows its foundation LLM: a decoder-only transformer trained with next-token-prediction-style objectives, augmented with a catalog-aware ranking head. The scoring head scores only in-catalog items. netflixtechblog . For very large catalogs, sampled softmax or candidate sets can make training and inference efficient. This constrains recommendations to the catalog while supporting efficient scoring over large candidate sets. netflixtechblog .

318.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
318.title: Results
318.content: Netflix reports: netflixtechblog . | Evaluation | Result | . | Offline ranking | GenRec outperformed the production ranker despite fewer input signals and labeled examples | . | Data efficiency | About 40 times fewer Phase-2 labeled examples | . | Offline MRR | About +1.6% improvement | . | Online test | Statistically significant short-term and long-term gains | . | Traffic coverage | About 10% of Netflix traffic | . | Test duration | About 4 weeks | . These results apply to Netflix’s production baseline, traffic, catalog, and evaluation setup. They demonstrate the potential of LLM-backed rankers, not a universal guarantee that an LLM ranker will outperform every existing recommender. netflixtechblog .

319.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
319.title: The broader shift
319.content: Netflix frames GenRec as a shift from feature engineering to context engineering. netflixtechblog . | Traditional RecSys | LLM-native RecSys | . | Dense feature vectors | Verbalized textual context | . | Hand-crafted features | Context construction from logs and metadata | . | Task-specific architectures | Shared foundation backbone | . | Sparse IDs and custom objectives | Data, verbalization, objectives, and rewards | . | Classic RecSys infrastructure | LLM-style GPU infrastructure, batching, and caching | . The prompt becomes a new kind of feature vector. Modeling effort shifts from designing features to deciding which signals to include, how far back in time to go, and how to compress history within a token budget. netflixtechblog .

320.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
320.title: Part 5: Cross-Cutting Design Patterns

321.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
321.title: Pattern 1: Separate hard constraints from soft relevance
321.content: A semantic model should not be responsible for enforcing every business rule. User query | +-- hard constraints --> deterministic filters | +-- semantic intent ---> vector retrieval | +-- ranking signals ---> learned ranker . Search-expert demonstrates this clearly: structured extraction enables hard filtering before semantic ranking. sarthakai.substack .

322.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
322.title: Pattern 2: Move expensive reasoning offline
322.content: A large model can explore, plan, and optimize during training. The deployed model should be as small and fast as the quality bar allows. Retrieve-for-Train uses offline reinforcement learning to discover good fan-out behavior, then distills it into a 53.9M-parameter diffusion retriever. research .

323.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
323.title: Pattern 3: Use catalog-aware constraints
323.content: LLMs can hallucinate out-of-catalog items. Recommendation and search systems should constrain outputs to valid, available, and business-approved candidates. GenRec uses a catalog-aware scoring head that scores only in-catalog items. netflixtechblog .

324.doc: Recommendation, Search, Retrieval, and Ranking in 2026
324.title: Pattern 4: Treat context as a budget
324.content: Long histories improve potential signal but increase cost. Context engineering is the process of choosing, compressing, ordering, and prioritizing context within a token budget. Netflix reduced context tokens to about one-third of the original budget with negligible offline ranking degradation. netflixtechblog .
